topics.title: How the web works: client, server, request, response
topics.summary: Every app you manage is a conversation between a client (browser or phone app) that asks and a server that answers. The client sends a request over the internet, the server does some work (often reading a database) and sends back a response.
topics.why: This is the mental model behind almost every engineering conversation: where a bug lives, why a page is slow, which team owns a failure. If you can trace one request end to end, you can follow any architecture discussion.
concepts: Packets and the network in between
What happens when you press Enter in the address bar
topics.do_it: Open any website, press F12, go to the Network tab and reload. Pick 3 requests and ask Claude to explain each one (who asked, who answered, what came back).
topics.prove: Talk for 2 minutes on "What happens when a user logs in?" without notes. Record yourself on your phone.
topics.interview: Walk me through what happens when a user types our URL and presses Enter.
covers: Frontend: how frontend talks to backend

topics.title: Frontend basics: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript
topics.summary: HTML is the structure of a page, CSS is how it looks, JavaScript makes it interactive. TypeScript is JavaScript with types added, so many mistakes are caught before the code runs.
topics.why: When a designer, a frontend developer and QA argue about a defect, you need to know whether it is a markup, styling or logic problem, and why teams choose TypeScript for larger codebases.
concepts: DOM: the page as a tree the browser can change
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to build a one-page 'project status card' in plain HTML/CSS/JS. Then ask it to change only the CSS, then only the JS, so you see the three layers separately.
topics.prove: Explain to a non-technical stakeholder why changing a button colour is a 10-minute job but changing what the button does may take days.
topics.interview: Why would a team move from JavaScript to TypeScript, and what does it cost?

topics.title: Frontend frameworks: React, Angular, Vue, Next.js
topics.summary: Frameworks are toolkits for building complex interfaces from reusable components. React is the most common; Angular is an all-in-one framework popular in enterprises; Vue is lighter; Next.js adds server rendering and routing on top of React.
topics.why: Framework choice affects hiring, speed of delivery and performance. You will be asked to weigh in on rewrites and migrations, and you need to know what 'components', 'props' and 'state' mean when developers estimate.
concepts: Hooks (React's way to use state and side effects)
topics.do_it: Ask Claude: 'Build a tiny React task list with add and complete'. Then ask it to label which parts are components, props and state.
topics.prove: Explain props vs state using a project-plan analogy in under 60 seconds.
topics.interview: Our team wants to rewrite an Angular app in React. What questions would you ask before agreeing?

topics.title: Rendering strategies: SPA, MPA, CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR
topics.summary: Rendering is where and when the HTML is produced. In the browser (CSR/SPA), on the server for every request (SSR), once at build time (SSG), or rebuilt on a schedule (ISR). An MPA reloads a full page per click.
topics.why: This choice drives SEO, page speed, hosting cost and complexity. Marketing pages, dashboards and product catalogues usually need different strategies, and the trade-off often shows up in your roadmap discussions.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to make a table: for an e-commerce site, which rendering strategy for home page, product page, cart and account dashboard, and why.
topics.prove: Explain why an SEO team might push back on a pure single-page app.
topics.interview: Product wants the catalogue to be fast and searchable on Google, but prices change hourly. What rendering approach would you discuss with engineering?
covers: SPA, MPA, SSR, CSR, SSG, ISR

topics.title: Web quality: responsive design, accessibility, performance, build tools
topics.summary: Responsive design adapts layouts to screen size. Accessibility (a11y) makes products usable by people with disabilities, measured against WCAG. Performance techniques include lazy loading, compression and minification. Build tools (Webpack, Vite, Babel) and package managers (npm, pnpm, Yarn) bundle and manage the code.
topics.why: Accessibility is often a legal and contractual requirement, and performance directly affects conversion. These are non-functional requirements you must put into acceptance criteria and release checklists.
topics.do_it: Run Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools > Lighthouse) on your company website. Paste the report summary into Claude and ask for the top 5 fixes ranked by user impact.
topics.prove: Write 3 accessibility acceptance criteria for a login form.
topics.interview: How do you make sure accessibility doesn't get dropped at the end of a release?
covers: Webpack, Vite, Babel, npm, pnpm, Yarn

topics.title: Backend basics: what the server side actually does
topics.summary: The backend receives requests, checks who is asking, applies business rules, reads or writes the database and returns a response. Code is usually split into controllers (handle the request), services (business logic) and data access.
topics.why: Most estimates, outages and data issues live in the backend. Knowing the layers lets you ask precise questions: is this a validation rule, a business rule or a data problem?
concepts: Synchronous vs asynchronous work (queues, background jobs)
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to draw (in text) the layers for 'user places an order' and to list which layer each failure would come from: card declined, out of stock, server timeout.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder why 'just add a field' can touch three layers and a database migration.
topics.interview: A feature looks small in the UI but engineering says 3 sprints. How do you find out why?

topics.title: Backend stacks: Node.js, Python, PHP and their frameworks
topics.summary: Common backend languages and frameworks: Node.js (Express, NestJS), Python (Django, Flask, FastAPI) and PHP (Laravel). They differ in speed, ecosystem, hiring pool and fit for AI work (Python dominates AI).
topics.why: You don't need to code them, but you will hear them in architecture reviews and staffing plans, and AI integrations often add a Python service alongside an existing stack.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude for a one-page comparison of Node/NestJS, Python/FastAPI and PHP/Laravel for a team adding an AI feature to an existing app.
topics.prove: Explain why AI teams often pick Python even when the main product is in another language.
topics.interview: How would the existing tech stack influence your plan to add an LLM feature?

topics.title: APIs and HTTP: methods, status codes, REST
topics.summary: An API is the contract one system uses to talk to another. REST APIs use HTTP methods (GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove) and return status codes (2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error).
topics.why: APIs are how every integration, mobile app and AI tool connects. Reading an API doc, understanding an error code and spotting a breaking change are core TPM skills.
concepts: HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
topics.do_it: Install Postman (or use your browser) and call a free public API such as a weather or country API. Ask Claude to explain each part of the request and response.
topics.prove: Explain an API to a business stakeholder using a restaurant-waiter analogy, then explain what a 401 vs a 500 means for who must fix it.
topics.interview: A partner says our API is 'broken'. How do you triage it in the first 15 minutes?

topics.title: JSON and data formats
topics.summary: JSON is the text format almost all modern APIs and AI tools use to send structured data: keys and values, lists and nested objects. A schema describes what shape the JSON must have.
topics.why: You will read JSON in API docs, logs, AI structured outputs and automation tools (Zapier, n8n). Validating that data matches the agreed schema prevents many integration bugs.
concepts: Objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to design the JSON for a 'project risk' record (id, title, owner, severity, mitigations list). Then deliberately break it and ask Claude to validate it.
topics.prove: Read an unfamiliar JSON API response and explain what each field means.
topics.interview: How would you make sure two teams agree on the data contract before they build?

topics.title: API styles: REST vs GraphQL vs WebSockets vs gRPC
topics.summary: REST: resources over HTTP. GraphQL: one endpoint, the client asks for exactly the fields it needs. WebSockets: a two-way live connection for chat and live updates. gRPC: fast binary calls, mostly between internal services.
topics.why: Teams argue about these choices. You should understand the trade-offs in complexity, performance, caching and tooling so you can help the team decide and document why.
concepts: When each is a good fit
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to recommend an API style for: a public partner API, a live chat feature, internal microservice calls, and a mobile app with slow networks. Challenge each answer.
topics.prove: Explain in one minute why a chat feature can't just use normal REST polling.
topics.interview: Engineering wants to introduce GraphQL. What benefits and risks would you put in the decision record?

topics.title: Webhooks, events and idempotency
topics.summary: A webhook is an automatic message one system sends to another when something happens (payment succeeded, form submitted). Because messages can be retried, receiving systems must be idempotent: handling the same message twice must not, for example, charge a customer twice.
topics.why: Payments, CRMs, automations and AI agents all rely on webhooks. Duplicate or lost events are a classic source of production incidents.
topics.do_it: Create a free Zapier or Make account and build a webhook trigger that posts a message when a Google Form is submitted. Then ask Claude what would happen if the webhook fired twice.
topics.prove: Explain idempotency using a 'pressing the lift button twice' analogy, then a real payment example.
topics.interview: Customers were double-charged after a gateway timeout. What questions do you ask engineering?

topics.title: Authentication vs authorization, sessions and JWT
topics.summary: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are; authorization (AuthZ) decides what you may do. After login, apps keep you signed in with a session or a token such as a JWT, which carries signed claims about the user.
topics.why: Security reviews, enterprise sales and AI agent permissions all hinge on these concepts. Many breaches come from authorization mistakes, not broken logins.
topics.do_it: Paste a sample JWT from jwt.io into its debugger. Ask Claude what each claim means and what would happen if the token never expired.
topics.prove: Explain the difference between AuthN and AuthZ with an office building analogy (badge vs which floors you can enter).
topics.interview: An enterprise client asks how our product controls who can see which records. What do you need to confirm with engineering?

topics.title: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SSO
topics.summary: OAuth 2.0 lets one app get limited access to another on a user's behalf ("Allow this app to read your calendar"). OpenID Connect adds login on top of OAuth. SSO lets employees use one company login for many apps, usually through an identity provider like Okta or Azure AD.
topics.why: Enterprise deals often require SSO. AI agents and MCP connectors use OAuth to act on a user's behalf, so you'll be scoping these flows.
concepts: OAuth roles: user, client app, authorization server, resource
SSO and identity providers (SAML vs OIDC)
topics.do_it: Use 'Sign in with Google' on any site, then ask Claude to map each screen you saw to the OAuth step happening behind it.
topics.prove: Draw the OAuth flow on paper from memory and explain it in 90 seconds.
topics.interview: A large customer requires SSO before signing. How would you scope and plan it?

topics.title: Databases: SQL vs NoSQL (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis)
topics.summary: Relational (SQL) databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL store data in tables with fixed schemas and strong consistency. NoSQL databases like MongoDB (documents) and Redis (key-value, in memory) trade some structure for flexibility and scale.
topics.why: Database choice affects data integrity, reporting, scale and migration effort. You need to follow these discussions and spot when a choice creates delivery risk.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to model the same 'project with tasks and owners' data as SQL tables and as MongoDB documents, then list pros and cons of each for your use case.
topics.prove: Explain to a finance stakeholder why their reporting team prefers SQL.
topics.interview: When would you push back on a team choosing NoSQL for transactional data?

topics.title: Data modelling: keys, relationships and ER diagrams
topics.summary: An ER diagram (ERD) shows the entities in a system (Customer, Order, Product), their attributes and how they relate: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many. Primary keys identify a row; foreign keys link rows across tables.
topics.why: Reading an ERD lets you check that requirements are actually supported by the data model, find hidden dependencies and estimate the impact of changes.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to generate an ERD (as a Mermaid diagram) for a simple project-management tool. Paste it into mermaid.live to see it, then ask it to add 'task dependencies' and note what changed.
topics.prove: Upload an ERD from your own project (anonymised) to Claude, ask for an explanation, then explain it back to Claude and ask it to grade you.
topics.interview: Here's an ERD. What would break if we allowed a task to have multiple owners?
covers: Semantic Search: upload ERD to AI and ask for explanation

topics.title: Queries, joins, indexes, transactions and ACID
topics.summary: Joins combine data from related tables. Indexes are like a book index: they make lookups fast but slow down writes and use storage. Transactions group changes so they all succeed or all fail; ACID describes those guarantees.
topics.why: 'The page is slow' is very often a missing index or a heavy query. Knowing this lets you ask the right questions instead of asking for 'more servers'.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain a slow query scenario: 'Find all overdue tasks for a user' on a table with 10 million rows. Ask what index would help and what the trade-off is.
topics.prove: Explain ACID using a bank transfer example.
topics.interview: Users report the dashboard takes 12 seconds to load. Engineering suggests a bigger database server. What do you ask first?
covers: Database Query Optimization (TPM level: ask the right questions)

topics.title: ORMs, migrations, backups and why DB changes affect the app
topics.summary: An ORM lets developers work with database rows as code objects. Schema changes are shipped as migrations. Connection pooling reuses database connections. Backups and point-in-time restore protect against data loss.
topics.why: Database migrations are one of the riskiest parts of a release. Rollback plans, downtime windows and data-loss risk land on your desk.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to write a release plan for 'rename a column used by 3 services' with zero downtime. Note each step and why order matters.
topics.prove: Explain to a non-technical stakeholder why a 'small database change' needs a release window and a rollback plan.
topics.interview: A migration failed halfway in production. What should already have been in the plan?
covers: Explain why DB changes affect app

topics.title: Scaling databases: replication, sharding, partitioning
topics.summary: Replication copies data to other servers (read replicas, failover). Partitioning splits a big table into parts. Sharding spreads data across many databases by a key such as customer region.
topics.why: These come up when a product grows fast. They are expensive, slow to change and affect every team, so they belong on the roadmap early.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude: 'Our SaaS has 5x'd customers in a year and the database is at 80% CPU. Give me options from cheapest to most complex.' Turn the answer into a one-slide decision summary.
topics.prove: Explain replication lag with a real symptom a user would see.
topics.interview: How would you plan a sharding project so it doesn't freeze feature delivery for six months?

topics.title: DNS, domains and nameservers
topics.summary: DNS is the internet's phone book: it turns names like example.com into IP addresses. Domains are bought from registrars, nameservers hold the records, and record types (A, CNAME, MX, TXT, SOA) point traffic and email to the right place. TTL controls how long answers are cached, which is why changes 'propagate' slowly.
topics.why: Launches, migrations and outages regularly involve DNS. Knowing TTL lets you plan cut-overs instead of waiting and hoping.
concepts: Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SOA
topics.do_it: Use a free DNS lookup site on your company domain. Paste the records into Claude and ask what each does.
topics.prove: Explain why you lower the TTL a day before a migration.
topics.interview: We're moving our website to a new host on Saturday. What DNS steps go into the plan?

topics.title: Email deliverability: SPF, DKIM, DMARC
topics.summary: SPF, DKIM and DMARC are DNS records that prove your emails really come from your domain, stopping spoofing and keeping your mail out of spam folders.
topics.why: Product emails (password resets, invoices, notifications) failing to arrive is a common launch blocker, and the fix sits across marketing, IT and engineering.
concepts: SPF: who may send for your domain
topics.do_it: Open any email in Gmail > Show original. Paste the authentication results into Claude and ask what passed and why it matters.
topics.prove: Explain in 60 seconds why password-reset emails might land in spam after moving to a new email provider.
topics.interview: Customers say they never get our onboarding emails. Who do you involve and what do you check?

topics.title: IP addresses: IPv4, IPv6, public, private, static
topics.summary: Every device on a network has an IP address. Public addresses are reachable from the internet; private ones are used inside networks. IPv6 exists because IPv4 addresses ran out. Static IPs don't change, which matters for allow-lists.
topics.why: Client firewalls, allow-listing, VPNs and cloud networking all depend on this. It often comes up when integrating with enterprise or banking clients.
topics.do_it: Search 'what is my IP' and compare with the private IP in your computer's network settings. Ask Claude to explain why they differ.
topics.prove: Explain why a bank client asks for our static IPs before integration.
topics.interview: An enterprise client's firewall blocks our webhooks. What information do you gather?
covers: Public IP, Private IP, Static IP

topics.title: Network protocols: TCP, UDP, HTTP(S), ports, sockets, SSH
topics.summary: TCP delivers data reliably and in order; UDP is faster but may drop data (used for video and gaming). HTTP and HTTPS run on top. Ports route traffic to the right program (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH). SSH is a secure way to log in to servers.
topics.why: Firewall changes, connectivity tickets and security audits use this vocabulary. You'll understand 'port 443 is blocked' or 'we need SSH access' immediately.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to make a cheat sheet of 10 common ports and what breaks if each is blocked.
topics.prove: Explain why video calls often use UDP.
topics.interview: A client's network team says 'only 443 outbound is allowed'. What does that mean for our product?

topics.title: HTTPS, TLS and certificates
topics.summary: HTTPS is HTTP encrypted with TLS (the successor of SSL). A certificate proves a site's identity and is issued by a certificate authority. Certificates expire and must be renewed.
topics.why: Expired certificates cause embarrassing, avoidable outages. Security questionnaires also ask about TLS versions and certificate management.
topics.do_it: Click the padlock on your company site and view the certificate. Ask Claude what each field means and when it expires.
topics.prove: Explain what users would see if our certificate expired tonight and who should own renewal.
topics.interview: How would you prevent certificate-expiry outages across 40 services?

topics.title: CORS, proxies and reverse proxies
topics.summary: CORS is a browser rule that controls which websites may call your API from JavaScript. A forward proxy sits in front of users; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers (for routing, caching, SSL and security).
topics.why: 'CORS error' is one of the most common blockers when frontend and backend teams integrate. Reverse proxies like Nginx appear in most architectures.
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain a real CORS error message and which team (frontend or backend) must fix it.
topics.prove: Explain why a CORS error can't be fixed from frontend code alone.
topics.interview: The frontend team is blocked by CORS errors two days before launch. How do you unblock it?

topics.title: CDN, load balancers and firewalls (WAF)
topics.summary: A CDN caches content on servers close to users for speed. A load balancer spreads traffic across servers and removes unhealthy ones. A firewall, and especially a web application firewall (WAF), blocks malicious traffic.
topics.why: These three sit in front of almost every production system. They affect performance, availability and security, and they often feature in incident timelines.
concepts: Load balancing algorithms and health checks
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to draw a request path: user > DNS > CDN > WAF > load balancer > app servers > database, and list what each layer protects against.
topics.prove: Explain why a CDN makes a site faster for users in India when servers are in the US.
topics.interview: Traffic will triple during a sale. Which layers do you check with the team?

topics.title: Private networks: subnets, NAT, gateways, VPN
topics.summary: Cloud networks are split into public subnets (reachable from the internet) and private subnets (for databases and internal services). NAT gateways let private servers reach out without being reachable. VPNs create encrypted tunnels into private networks.
topics.why: Security reviews and cloud cost discussions mention these constantly. Understanding them lets you follow infrastructure designs and client connectivity requirements.
concepts: Zero Trust as the modern alternative
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain a three-tier network: load balancer in public subnet, app servers and database in private subnets. Ask why the database should never be public.
topics.prove: Explain why 'the database is in a private subnet' is a good answer in a security questionnaire.
topics.interview: A client wants a private connection to our platform instead of the public internet. What options would you explore?

topics.title: What an LLM is, and your first API call
topics.summary: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. That simple objective, at scale, produces models that can write, reason, summarise and use tools. You can use them through chat apps or through an API.
topics.why: Every AI product decision you make rests on this mental model: what the model really is, what it can't know, and why answers vary.
topics.do_it: Create a free Gemini API key in Google AI Studio and keep it private. Use AI Studio's prompt screen, then click 'Get code' and ask Claude to explain every line of that code.
topics.prove: Explain to a sceptical executive what an LLM is and isn't in 2 minutes, without jargon.
topics.interview: What's the difference between using ChatGPT and building on an LLM API?
covers: REST API, SDK, API Key (first use)

topics.title: How LLMs are built: pre-training, fine-tuning, RLHF
topics.summary: LLMs are first pre-trained on internet-scale text (expensive, months, many GPUs), producing a base model. They are then post-trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to become helpful assistants.
topics.why: This explains why models have knowledge cut-offs, why they sound confident when wrong, and why training your own model is rarely the right project.
topics.do_it: Watch the first hour of Karpathy's deep dive. Ask Claude to quiz you with 10 questions on the training pipeline.
topics.prove: Explain why a model doesn't know about last week's news, and the two ways to fix that (search/RAG or retraining).
topics.interview: A stakeholder wants us to 'train our own ChatGPT'. How do you respond?

topics.title: Transformers and attention (concept level)
topics.summary: The transformer is the neural network design behind modern LLMs. Its key idea, attention, lets every word look at every other word to work out context, and it processes text in parallel, which made huge training runs possible.
topics.why: You don't need the maths, but you'll understand why context length is expensive, why models are fast on GPUs, and what people mean by 'attention' and 'KV cache'.
concepts: Why attention cost grows with context length
topics.do_it: Read The Illustrated Transformer with Claude open. After each section, explain it back to Claude in your own words and ask for corrections.
topics.prove: Explain attention using a meeting analogy: everyone listens to the people most relevant to their point.
topics.interview: Why do longer prompts cost more and run slower?

topics.title: Tokens and tokenization
topics.summary: Models read and write tokens, small chunks of text (roughly 3–4 English characters each). Prices, limits and speed are all measured in tokens. Different models split text differently, and non-English text often uses more tokens.
topics.why: Every AI budget, rate limit and context limit is in tokens. You'll estimate costs and explain why the same feature costs more in Hindi than in English.
concepts: Rough rule: 1 token ≈ ¾ word in English
Rate limits in tokens per minute
topics.do_it: Paste the same paragraph in English and in Hindi into the tokenizer tool. Compare counts and ask Claude why they differ.
topics.prove: Estimate how many tokens a 10-page requirements document is, and show your working.
topics.interview: Our AI feature's costs are double the estimate. What token-related causes would you check?

topics.title: Context window
topics.summary: The context window is the model's working memory: everything it can see at once, including instructions, conversation history, documents and its own answer. Anything outside the window is invisible to the model.
topics.why: It decides whether a model can read a whole contract, how long a chat stays coherent, and why agents need memory strategies. Bigger windows also cost more per request.
topics.do_it: Give Claude a long document and ask a question about a detail near the start, then near the end. Ask Claude to explain how context windows affect what it 'remembers'.
topics.prove: Explain to a stakeholder why the chatbot 'forgot' something the user said an hour ago.
topics.interview: When would you load a whole document into context versus using retrieval?

topics.title: Prompting fundamentals
topics.summary: Prompting is how you specify the task to a model: clear goal, context, constraints, examples and the output format you want. Good prompts read like a good brief to a capable new colleague.
topics.why: This is the skill you'll use daily to write PRDs, user stories, analysis and code with AI. It's also how you'll review prompts your team ships into products.
concepts: Be clear and direct; give the why
topics.do_it: Take one recurring task (weekly status report). Write a prompt, run it 3 times, score the outputs against 5 criteria, improve the prompt, and save the before/after in a document.
topics.prove: Show a before and after prompt and explain each change.
topics.interview: How would you make prompt quality measurable rather than a matter of opinion?

topics.title: Advanced prompting techniques
topics.summary: Beyond basics: role or system prompts, structured prompts with XML tags, asking the model to think step by step, chaining prompts into a pipeline, and asking for structured output such as JSON.
topics.why: These techniques turn one-off chats into reliable workflows, and they're what product prompts and agents are built from.
topics.do_it: Build a 3-step prompt chain: (1) extract requirements from meeting notes, (2) turn them into user stories, (3) write acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then. Save it as a reusable template.
topics.prove: Demonstrate the chain on a new set of notes and explain why chaining beats one giant prompt.
topics.interview: How would you version and test prompts that run inside our product?
covers: AI Coding Assistants (AI for stories and ACs)

topics.title: Hallucinations and how to reduce them
topics.summary: A hallucination is a confident but false or unsupported output. It happens because models generate plausible text rather than look up facts. You reduce it by allowing 'I don't know', grounding answers in provided sources, asking for quotes and citations, and verifying.
topics.why: Hallucination risk is the first question executives, legal and customers ask about AI features. You need a clear, honest mitigation plan.
topics.do_it: Ask a model 5 questions about an obscure topic with and without a source document attached. Log which answers were wrong and which mitigation fixed them.
topics.prove: Present a one-slide 'Hallucination mitigation plan' for a customer-facing chatbot.
topics.interview: Legal is worried our AI will make things up. What controls do you propose?

topics.title: Grounding
topics.summary: Grounding means tying the model's answer to trusted sources (your documents, a database, search results) instead of its general training memory, ideally with citations so people can check.
topics.why: Grounded answers are what make enterprise AI trustworthy and auditable. It's the bridge between hallucination risk and RAG.
topics.do_it: Upload 3 project documents to NotebookLM and ask 10 questions. Check every citation it gives against the source.
topics.prove: Explain grounding to a stakeholder using an 'open-book exam' analogy.
topics.interview: How would you prove to an auditor that our assistant's answers come from approved documents?

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.summary: An embedding turns text (or images) into a list of numbers that captures meaning. Texts with similar meaning end up close together, so 'cheap flights' and 'low-cost airfare' match even with no shared words.
topics.why: Embeddings power semantic search, RAG, recommendations and duplicate detection. Choosing an embedding model affects quality, cost and language support.
concepts: Re-embedding cost when you switch models
topics.do_it: Ask Claude to explain, with a toy 2D example, how 'king', 'queen', 'apple' and 'banana' would sit in embedding space. Then read the Gemini embeddings docs and ask Claude to explain the sample code.
topics.prove: Explain why semantic search finds results that keyword search misses.
topics.interview: We want to switch embedding models. What's the migration cost and risk?

topics.title: Vector databases

p: A language model only knows what was in its training data. It has never seen your HR policies, your product docs or last week's release notes, and its knowledge stops at a cut-off date. Ask it about your leave policy and it will either say it doesn't know or, worse, produce a confident answer that sounds right and isn't.

You could paste the whole policy handbook into every prompt, but that gets slow and expensive, and many document sets are far bigger than any context window. You could retrain the model on your documents, but that is costly, slow to update and still doesn't reliably make the model quote the right clause.

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) takes a simpler route: at the moment a question is asked, find the few passages that are most likely to contain the answer, hand them to the model together with the question, and tell it to answer only from them. Think of it as turning a closed-book exam into an open-book exam where someone hands the student the right three pages.

sections.h: How it works, step by step
p: A RAG system has two halves. The indexing half runs ahead of time, whenever documents are added or change. The answering half runs every time a user asks something.
sections.flowLabel: RAG pipeline: indexing ahead of time, then answering each question
steps: Documents are cut into passages of a few hundred words. Too small and a passage loses its meaning; too large and the right sentence is buried in noise.
Each chunk is turned into an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning, using an embedding model.
Embeddings are saved in a vector database together with the original text and metadata such as document name, date and who is allowed to see it.

When a question arrives it is embedded the same way, and the database returns the closest chunks (the 'top-k', often 3 to 10). Many teams combine this with keyword search so exact terms like policy numbers are not missed.
A second, more careful model re-orders those candidates so the very best passages come first.
The model receives the question, the retrieved passages and instructions such as 'answer only from these sources, cite them, and say so if the answer is not there'.

sections.h: Worked example: an HR policy assistant
p: An employee asks: "Can I carry over unused leave to next year?"

Retrieval searches 400 pages of HR documents and returns three chunks: the leave policy section on carry-over, a 2025 policy update that changed the limit, and a FAQ entry. The model is then prompted: "Using only the sources below, answer the question. Quote the clause you rely on. If sources conflict, prefer the most recent and say so."

The answer: "Yes, up to 10 days, which must be used by 31 March (Leave Policy update, Jan 2025, section 4.2). The older handbook says 5 days; the 2025 update replaces it." The employee can click the citation and check.
Notice that the quality of this answer depended almost entirely on retrieval. If the 2025 update had not been retrieved, the model would have confidently given the old, wrong limit.

sections.h: Where RAG fails, and how teams fix it
table: "I couldn't find that" or a wrong answer
Better chunking, hybrid keyword + semantic search, reranking
Answer misses who or what the passage is about
Add a short summary of the document to each chunk before embedding (Anthropic's contextual retrieval)
Remove superseded documents, store dates as metadata, tell the model to prefer the newest
Confident answer not supported by citations
Stricter instructions, require quotes, automated groundedness checks
Filter retrieval by the user's permissions before anything reaches the model
Retrieve more chunks, break the question into steps, or use an agent
p: Anthropic reported that adding context to each chunk cut failed retrievals by 49%, and by 67% when combined with reranking. The lesson for a TPM: most RAG quality work is search work, not prompt work.

sections.h: What a TPM must decide and track
bullets: Scope the corpus: which documents, who owns them, how often they change, and who removes outdated ones. Content ownership is the most common gap.
Permissions: does every user see every document? If not, access control must be part of retrieval from day one.
Build or buy: a managed product (for example an enterprise search assistant) versus your own pipeline with a vector database.
Quality bar: build a set of 50 to 100 real questions with known correct answers before launch, and measure against it every release.
Cost drivers: embedding all documents once (cheap), re-embedding when you change models, and per-question cost, which grows with how many chunks you send.
Failure behaviour: what the assistant should say when it doesn't know, and how users report wrong answers.
Owners: who fixes a wrong answer? Usually it is a content owner, not an engineer.

gloss: A passage cut from a larger document, the unit that gets retrieved.
Numbers that represent the meaning of text, so similar meanings sit close together.
A store optimised for finding the nearest embeddings quickly.
The number of best-matching chunks retrieved for each question.
Combining keyword search with semantic (embedding) search.
A second pass that re-orders retrieved chunks by relevance.
Tying the answer to supplied sources rather than the model's memory.
How well an answer is supported by the retrieved sources; a key quality metric.

quiz: Why is RAG usually preferred over fine-tuning for a company knowledge base?

Because the knowledge changes often and must be citable. RAG updates by re-indexing documents in minutes, keeps answers traceable to sources, and respects permissions at retrieval time. Fine-tuning is slow to update and doesn't reliably reproduce exact facts.
Users say the assistant gives an old policy. Name two likely causes.
The outdated document is still indexed (no content owner removed it), or both versions were retrieved and the model wasn't told to prefer the newest, often because dates weren't stored as metadata.
What does 'top-k = 5' mean, and what happens if you raise it to 30?
Five best-matching chunks are sent to the model. At 30 you may catch more relevant passages, but cost and latency rise and irrelevant text can distract the model.
Why might pure semantic search miss 'Policy HR-114'?
Embeddings capture meaning, not exact strings, so a code like HR-114 may not be close to anything. Keyword search catches exact identifiers, which is why hybrid search is common.
Before launch, what single artefact best protects quality?
A golden set of real questions with known correct answers, run against every change to prompts, chunking or models.

p: Every app you have ever managed works the same basic way. A client, which is the browser or the mobile app on someone's phone, asks for something. A server, a computer in a data centre or the cloud, works out the answer and sends it back. That round trip is called a request and a response, and it happens dozens of times every time someone opens a page.

The client never touches the database directly. It only talks to servers through agreed addresses. That separation is why teams can be split into frontend and backend, and why so many incidents are about one side waiting for the other.

sections.h: What happens when you press Enter
sections.flowLabel: Request path from browser to server and back
steps: The browser splits https://shop.example.com/login?ref=ad into protocol (https), domain (shop.example.com), path (/login) and query (ref=ad).
DNS turns the domain into an IP address, like looking a name up in a phone book.
The browser connects to that IP and agrees encryption keys (TLS) so nobody in between can read the traffic.
It sends an HTTP request: a method (GET), the path, headers (browser type, cookies) and sometimes a body.
Application code checks who you are, reads the database, applies business rules and builds a response.
The browser receives HTML, CSS, JavaScript and data, often triggering more requests for images and scripts, and draws the page.

sections.h: Worked example: a user logs in
p: The user types email and password and presses Log in. The browser sends a POST request to /api/login with those details, encrypted by HTTPS.
The backend looks up the user, checks the password hash, and if it matches creates a session or token. It responds with status 200 and a cookie or token. If the password is wrong it returns 401.

The browser stores the token and, on every following request, sends it along so the server knows who is asking. The frontend then requests /api/dashboard, which returns the user's data as JSON, and the page fills in.
So 'login is slow' could mean DNS, the network, the password check, the database, or the dashboard call afterwards. Knowing the path tells you which team to ask.

table: Network, server overloaded or slow database
Looks broken but data is there

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask 'where in the request path does it fail?' before asking 'who broke it?'.
Use the browser's Network tab in triage calls; it shows each request, its status and its time.
Make sure architecture diagrams show the request path, not just boxes.
Define performance targets per step (for example API response under 300 ms) so they can be owned.

p: In a triage call, the fastest way to cut through 'the site is broken' is to ask someone to open the Network tab and read out the failing request: its URL, status code and time. Within a minute you usually know whether it's DNS (nothing loads), the backend (5xx), permissions (401/403) or the frontend (all requests succeed but the page looks wrong). That one habit saves hours of people talking past each other.

In planning, the request path is also how you split work and ownership. A new 'export report' feature means a button (frontend), an endpoint (backend), a query (database), maybe a background job and an email. Mapping the path on a whiteboard before estimation exposes the hidden pieces, like the job queue, that otherwise surface mid-sprint.

mis: The website and the app are separate systems.
They usually share the same backend APIs; only the client differs.
If the page loads, the backend is fine.
The page shell can load from a CDN while data calls fail.
Slowness is always the server's fault.
It can be DNS, network, large images or heavy JavaScript in the browser.

gloss: The program making requests: browser or mobile app.
One question and its answer over the network.
The full address of a resource.
The language of web requests; HTTPS is the encrypted version.
How long a round trip takes.

quiz: Name the four parts of https://app.example.com/report?id=7
Protocol https, domain app.example.com, path /report, query id=7.
Why can't the browser just read the database directly?
For security and control: the server enforces who can see what and applies business rules. Exposing the database would let anyone read or change data.
A user says login is slow. Give three places the delay could be.
DNS lookup, the authentication check or database on the server, or the dashboard data call that follows login.
What does the Network tab in DevTools show you?
Every request the page makes, its status code, size and how long it took.
What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
HTTPS encrypts the traffic using TLS so it can't be read or changed in transit.

sections.h: Three layers of every web page
p: Think of a web page like a building. HTML is the structure: walls, rooms, doors, meaning headings, paragraphs, buttons and form fields. CSS is the interior design: colours, fonts, spacing, layout. JavaScript is the electricity and plumbing: what happens when you click, type or scroll.

TypeScript is JavaScript with labels added to every piece of data, saying what type it is (number, text, list). The computer checks those labels before the code runs, which catches a whole class of bugs early.

sections.h: How the browser builds a page
steps: The browser turns the HTML into a tree of elements called the DOM.
Style rules are matched to elements to decide how each looks and where it sits.
Scripts can read and change the DOM, respond to clicks and fetch data from APIs.
Every change JavaScript makes can cause the browser to recalculate layout and paint again, which is why heavy scripts make pages sluggish.

p: HTML: <button>Submit</button> puts a button on the page.
CSS: makes it blue, rounded, and moves it to the right on desktop but full-width on mobile.
JavaScript: when clicked, validates the form, shows a spinner, calls the API and shows a success message or an error.
A request to 'make the button green' is CSS, minutes of work. 'Make the button also save a draft' is JavaScript plus probably a new API: days. Same button, very different estimates.

table: Safer at scale, more upfront typing
Hand-written CSS vs a design system
Logic in the frontend vs backend
Single source of truth, more secure
p: Rule of thumb: anything about security or money must be enforced on the backend, even if the frontend also checks it.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Split UI tickets into structure, style and behaviour when estimating.
Ask whether validation is duplicated on the backend for anything important.
Know that a TypeScript migration is a multi-sprint investment that pays off in fewer bugs.

p: Design reviews go faster when you separate the three layers. When a designer's mock-up shows a new card style, ask: is this pure CSS within the design system, or does it imply new behaviour like expand/collapse or inline editing? The first is a style ticket; the second needs JavaScript, state and possibly an API. Writing them as separate stories keeps estimates honest and lets a junior developer pick up the CSS work.

When a team proposes moving to TypeScript, ask for an incremental plan: TypeScript can be adopted file by file. The benefit shows up as fewer production bugs of the 'undefined is not a function' kind, so agree to measure defect rates before and after.

mis: HTML is a programming language.
It's markup: it describes structure, it doesn't compute anything.
Frontend validation is enough.
Users can bypass the browser; the backend must validate too.
TypeScript makes the app faster.
It makes development safer; runtime speed is the same JavaScript.

gloss: Rules that define appearance and layout.
The programming language that runs in browsers.
The browser's live tree of page elements.

quiz: Which layer would you change to fix overlapping text on mobile?
CSS (layout and responsive rules).
Why must a discount rule be enforced on the backend?
Anything in the browser can be changed by the user, so security and money rules must be checked on the server.
What is the main benefit of TypeScript?
Type errors are caught before the code runs, reducing bugs in large codebases.
What is the DOM?
The browser's tree of page elements, which JavaScript can read and change.
Why can a 'small' UI change take days?
If it changes behaviour, it may need new JavaScript logic, new APIs, tests and backend changes.

p: Plain JavaScript gets messy fast in a large app: hundreds of buttons, lists and forms that must stay in sync with changing data. Frameworks give a structure: build the UI from small reusable pieces called components, and let the framework update the screen when data changes.

React (from Meta) is the most widely used. Angular (from Google) is a complete, opinionated framework favoured in large enterprises. Vue is lighter and easy to adopt. Next.js is built on React and adds routing, server rendering and API routes, which is why it is common for full products.

sections.h: Core ideas you'll hear in stand-ups
steps: Self-contained building blocks like Header, TaskCard, DatePicker. A page is a tree of components.
Data passed into a component from its parent, like arguments: <TaskCard title='Review PRD' owner='Asha' />.
Data a component remembers and can change, like whether a dropdown is open or what's typed in a search box. When state changes, the component re-renders.
React functions (useState, useEffect) that let components hold state and run side effects such as fetching data.
Data many components need (logged-in user, cart). Stored in a shared store such as Redux, Zustand or React Context.

sections.h: Worked example: a project task board
p: The board page contains Column components; each Column contains TaskCard components. The list of tasks is fetched once and passed down as props.
When a user drags a card to Done, the board's state updates; React re-renders only the affected cards. If the change must persist, a hook calls the API to save it.
When a developer says 'the card doesn't update after save', they're telling you the state wasn't refreshed after the API call: a frontend state bug, not a database one.

table: More moving parts on the server
p: Rewrites between frameworks are expensive and rarely justified by the framework alone; push for a clear business reason.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask for a component inventory before estimating a redesign.
Treat a framework migration as a programme: incremental, page by page, with measurable goals.
Clarify where state lives when bugs involve 'stale' data.

p: When estimating UI work in a React or Angular codebase, ask whether the needed components already exist in the design system. A screen assembled from existing components might be two days; one needing three new components, each with states, accessibility and tests, might be two weeks. A component inventory turns vague UI estimates into countable work.

State bugs are among the most common frontend defects: a list that doesn't refresh, a badge count that's wrong after navigation, a form that keeps old values. When you see these, the fix is usually about where state lives and when it's refreshed after API calls, which is useful vocabulary for writing precise bug reports.

mis: React and Angular are interchangeable.
Angular is a full framework with built-in structure; React is a library you assemble with other tools.
Moving frameworks will fix our quality problems.
Quality problems usually come from process and architecture, which a rewrite doesn't change.
More components means a more complex app.
Small reusable components usually make apps simpler to change.

gloss: React function for state and side effects.
Redrawing a component after its data changes.

quiz: Props vs state in one sentence each?
Props are data given to a component by its parent; state is data the component owns and can change.
What is Next.js relative to React?
A framework on top of React adding routing, server rendering and backend features.
A card doesn't show the new status after saving. Where do you look first?
Frontend state management: whether the component's state is updated after the API call succeeds.
Why are framework rewrites risky?
They take long, freeze features, and the benefit is often unclear unless tied to measurable goals.
Name one reason an enterprise might choose Angular.
It provides a complete, consistent structure for large teams.

p: Rendering means producing the HTML the user sees. It can happen in the user's browser, on a server for every visit, or once in advance. Each choice trades speed, freshness, SEO and cost.

steps: Every click loads a new full page from the server. Simple and SEO-friendly, but feels slower.
The server sends a nearly empty page plus JavaScript; the browser builds everything. Feels app-like after load, but first load is slower and search engines may see less.
The server builds the full HTML for each request. Fast first view and good SEO, but more server work.
Pages are built once at deploy time and served as files from a CDN. Fastest and cheapest, but content is only as fresh as the last build.
Static pages that rebuild themselves in the background every few minutes. A middle ground.
After server-rendered HTML arrives, JavaScript 'wakes it up' to make it interactive.

table: Changes rarely, must be fast and indexable
Needs SEO; price and stock change
Personal; SSR if first-load speed matters
p: Modern frameworks like Next.js let teams mix these per page, which is now the norm.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Tie the choice to business goals: SEO traffic, conversion, personalisation.
Ask how long content can be stale before it hurts (that decides SSG vs ISR vs SSR).
Include Core Web Vitals or page-speed targets in acceptance criteria.

p: Rendering strategy often comes up when marketing complains about SEO or product complains about load time. Bring data: Google Search Console shows indexing problems, and Lighthouse shows load metrics such as Largest Contentful Paint. Then the conversation is about which pages need server rendering, not a whole-app rewrite.

When content changes, ask how fast it must show up. A price change that takes ten minutes to appear may be fine for a blog but unacceptable for a flash sale. That freshness requirement directly selects between static, incremental and server rendering, and it belongs in your requirements.

mis: SPAs are always faster.
They feel fast after loading, but the first load is often slower.
SSR is always better for SEO, so use it everywhere.
It adds server cost; static pages are better for content that rarely changes.
You must pick one strategy for the whole app.
Modern frameworks mix strategies per page.

gloss: Single-page application; JavaScript swaps views without full reloads.
Rendering on the server per request.

quiz: Why might SEO suffer with pure CSR?
Search engines may see a nearly empty page before JavaScript runs.
Which strategy suits a blog that changes weekly?
SSG (or ISR).
Prices change hourly on product pages that must rank on Google. Option?
ISR with a short refresh interval, or SSR.
What is hydration?
Making server-rendered HTML interactive by attaching JavaScript in the browser.
What's the main cost of SSR?
More server work and infrastructure per request.

sections.h: Quality you can't see in a demo
p: Some requirements never show up in a feature demo but decide whether a product succeeds: does it work on every screen size, can people with disabilities use it, and does it load fast on a cheap phone on a slow network? These are non-functional requirements, and they are easy to drop under deadline pressure.

steps: Layouts adapt to screen width using flexible grids and breakpoints. Designers usually provide mobile, tablet and desktop versions.
Usable with a keyboard, a screen reader, zoom and colour-blindness. Measured against WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines), levels A, AA and AAA; AA is the usual contractual target.
Lazy loading (load images only when they scroll into view), compression (gzip/brotli), minification (removing spaces from code) and image optimisation.
Bundlers (Webpack, Vite) combine and optimise files; Babel translates modern JavaScript for older browsers; package managers (npm, pnpm, Yarn) install third-party libraries.

p: Accessibility acceptance criteria for a login form might read: every field has a visible label read aloud by screen readers; the form can be completed using only the keyboard with a visible focus outline; error messages are announced and say how to fix the problem; text contrast meets WCAG AA (4.5:1).
Performance criteria: page interactive within 3 seconds on a mid-range phone on 4G; total page weight under 1 MB.

table: Add a11y checks to Definition of Done

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Put accessibility and performance into acceptance criteria, not a separate 'later' ticket.
Ask whether contracts or regulations require WCAG AA.
Track page speed (Lighthouse scores) as a release metric.

p: Accessibility gaps found during UAT or by a customer audit are expensive: they often require rework across many screens. The cheapest place to catch them is in design (contrast, focus states, labels) and in the Definition of Done (keyboard test, screen-reader smoke test, automated checks). In regulated industries and government contracts, WCAG compliance can be a legal requirement, so check early.

Performance tends to erode silently: each release adds a library or a large image. Teams that hold the line set a performance budget, for example JavaScript under 300 KB and LCP under 2.5 seconds on mobile, and fail the build when it's exceeded. As a TPM you can make that budget a visible release criterion.

mis: Accessibility only matters for a few users.
It affects many users (ageing, temporary injuries, situational limits) and is often a legal requirement.
Automated tools catch all accessibility issues.
They catch only a portion; manual keyboard and screen-reader checks are needed.
Package managers are a developer detail.
Third-party packages are a major security and licensing risk.

gloss: Shrinking code by removing unneeded characters.
Tool that packages code for the browser.

quiz: What WCAG level is the usual contractual target?
AA.
Name two performance techniques.
Lazy loading and compression (also minification, image optimisation).
What does a bundler do?
Combines and optimises code files for delivery to the browser.
Write one keyboard accessibility criterion.
All actions can be completed using only the keyboard with a visible focus indicator.
How do you stop performance degrading over time?
Set a performance budget and check it automatically in every build.

p: The backend is where the rules live. It receives requests from apps, checks who is asking, decides whether they're allowed, applies business logic (prices, approvals, workflows), reads and writes the database, talks to other systems, and returns a response. The frontend shows things; the backend decides things.

steps: Front door: routes requests to the right service, checks tokens, applies rate limits.
Reads the incoming request, validates input, calls the right service, formats the response.
The business logic: 'an order over ₹50,000 needs manager approval'.
Reads and writes the database, often through an ORM.
Slow work (emails, reports, AI calls) put on a queue and processed later, so users don't wait.

p: Controller receives POST /orders with items and address, checks the fields are present.
Service checks stock, calculates price and tax, applies the discount, reserves inventory, calls the payment provider.
Data layer saves the order in a transaction. A background job sends the confirmation email.
Failures map cleanly: card declined comes from the payment integration; out of stock from the service rules; a timeout from a slow database or provider. Each has a different owner and fix.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: When a 'small' feature has a big estimate, ask which layers it touches.
Ask what happens if a downstream service is slow: does the user wait or is it queued?
Make sure business rules are documented once, in the service layer, not scattered.

p: Backend estimates feel opaque until you ask about layers. 'Add an approval step for orders over a threshold' touches the service rules, a new status in the database, a notification job, API changes for the frontend, and reporting. Asking 'what changes in each layer?' turns a mysterious three-sprint estimate into a list you can prioritise or phase.

Queues are worth understanding because they change failure behaviour. If emails are queued, an email provider outage doesn't break checkout; mails are delayed and retried. If they're sent synchronously, checkout fails. Asking 'is this synchronous or queued?' during design reviews prevents a class of outages.

mis: Business logic lives in the database.
Mostly it lives in the service layer; the database stores data.
Background jobs are optional extras.
They're essential for reliability and speed in most systems.
An API gateway is just a proxy.
It often enforces authentication, rate limits and routing for everything.

gloss: Code that handles an incoming request.
A list of jobs processed in the background.
Single entry point that routes and secures API traffic.

quiz: Which layer holds 'orders over ₹50,000 need approval'?
The service (business logic) layer.
Why put email sending on a queue?
So the user doesn't wait, and failures can be retried without breaking the order.
What does an API gateway typically do?
Routes requests, checks authentication and applies rate limits.
Card declined vs timeout: which teams?
Declined is payment integration logic; timeout points to performance of the database or provider.
Why can 'add one field' be big?
It may touch the UI, API contract, service logic, database migration and reports.

p: Backends can be written in many languages. Three you'll meet most: JavaScript/TypeScript on Node.js, Python, and PHP. Each has frameworks that give structure, like a house plan gives structure to bricks.

table: Same language as the frontend; great for real-time and APIs
Django (batteries included), Flask (minimal), FastAPI (modern, fast APIs)
Dominant in AI, data and ML
Huge web footprint, fast to build CRUD apps

sections.h: Worked example: adding an AI feature
p: Your product's backend is in PHP/Laravel. The AI team wants Python because the best AI libraries are Python-first. A common pattern: keep the main app as is and add a small Python FastAPI service that the Laravel app calls over an internal API.
That decision adds a new deployment, monitoring and on-call surface, all of which belong in your plan.

Node.js handles many waiting connections efficiently (non-blocking). Python and PHP traditionally process requests one at a time per worker, though FastAPI and modern setups support async. For AI features, which mostly wait on model APIs, async handling matters for cost and throughput.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Stack choices are hiring and operations decisions, not just technical ones.
Adding a language means new CI, monitoring and skills: budget for it.
Ask 'what does the existing team know well?' before endorsing a new stack.

p: Stack decisions come up in hiring plans, vendor evaluations and AI initiatives. When engineering proposes a new language, ask about the full lifecycle: who builds it, who's on call at 2 a.m., how it's deployed and monitored, and how security patches are applied. A second language can double operational surface area.

For AI features, a small Python service beside the main application is a common, sensible pattern. Plan it as a real service: its own repository, CI pipeline, monitoring, API contract with the main app, and an owner. Teams often treat it as a side script and regret it in production.

mis: Python is too slow for production.
It runs large production systems; speed depends more on design.
PHP is outdated.
Modern PHP with Laravel powers many active products.
Choosing the 'best' language matters most.
Team skills and ecosystem fit usually matter more.

gloss: Structure and tools for building apps.

quiz: Why does AI work favour Python?
Most AI and ML libraries and examples are Python-first.
Express vs NestJS?
Express is minimal; NestJS adds structure for large teams.
What's the hidden cost of adding a Python service?
New deployment, monitoring, on-call and skills.
What is MVC?
An architecture separating data (model), UI (view) and request handling (controller).
Why does async matter for AI features?
They spend most time waiting on model APIs; async lets one server handle many such waits.

p: An API (application programming interface) is a promise one system makes to others: 'send me a request in this shape to this address, and I'll respond in this shape'. Your mobile app, your partners, your AI agents and your automations all depend on these promises. Break the promise without warning and things fail elsewhere.
Most web APIs are REST APIs over HTTP. They treat data as resources with addresses, like /orders/123, and use standard verbs to act on them.

sections.h: The parts of an API call
steps: What you want to do: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH update part, DELETE remove.
Extra information such as the API key or token (Authorization) and the data format (Content-Type: application/json).
The data you send, usually JSON, for POST/PUT/PATCH.
The first thing to read in a response.
The data returned, or an error message.

table: Caller slows down, or limit raised
p: Rule of thumb: 4xx is the caller's problem, 5xx is the provider's.

sections.h: Worked example: triaging 'your API is broken'
p: A partner says integration is failing. First question: what status code and when did it start?

401s since this morning: their key expired or was rotated. 429s: they're sending more than their plan allows. 500s for everyone: our incident. 400s after our release yesterday: we probably made a breaking change, for example renaming a field.
Breaking changes (removing or renaming fields, changing types) need versioning such as /v2/ and a deprecation period. Adding an optional field is non-breaking.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Insist on an API contract (OpenAPI/Swagger spec) before parallel frontend and backend work starts.
Have a versioning and deprecation policy and communicate it to partners.
Track error rates by status code family on a dashboard.
Know your rate limits and your vendors' limits; they become capacity constraints.

p: Most integration delays come from unclear contracts. Before frontend, backend or partner teams start building, ask for an OpenAPI spec with example requests and responses, error formats and status codes. Mock servers can be generated from it, so teams build in parallel and integration week becomes a formality.

Put an API change policy in writing: what counts as breaking, how much notice partners get, how versions are named, and how long old versions live. When something breaks for a partner, that policy is the difference between a quick, calm fix and an escalation to leadership.

mis: A 200 response means everything worked.
Some APIs return 200 with an error inside the body; read the response.
REST means any HTTP API.
REST is a specific resource-oriented style; many 'REST APIs' only loosely follow it.
Rate limits are only the provider's concern.
They're capacity limits you must plan around.

gloss: A style of API built on resources and HTTP methods.
The data in a request or response body.
A change that makes existing callers fail.
Cap on how many requests a caller may send in a period.
A standard format for describing APIs.

quiz: 401: not authenticated (who are you?). 403: authenticated but not allowed.
Which method creates a new record?
POST.
Is adding an optional response field a breaking change?
No, existing callers keep working.
A partner gets 429s. What does it mean?
They exceeded the rate limit; they must slow down or get a higher limit.
Why agree an OpenAPI spec early?
So frontend, backend and partners can build in parallel against the same contract.

p: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is plain text that represents structured data. Nearly every modern API, configuration file, automation tool and AI structured output uses it. If you can read JSON, you can read most of what flows between systems.

steps: Strings in double quotes, numbers, true/false, null, or nested objects and arrays.
Objects inside objects: a project contains a list of tasks, each with an owner object.
A description of what shape the JSON must have: required fields, types and allowed values.

p: {"id": "RSK-12", "title": "Vendor API rate limit", "severity": "high", "owner": {"name": "Ravi", "team": "Integrations"}, "mitigations": ["Request higher tier", "Add caching"], "closed": false}

Read it like a form: a risk with an id, title, severity, a nested owner, a list of mitigations and a yes/no closed flag. A schema would say severity must be one of low, medium, high and that id is required.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask for example request and response JSON in every integration spec.
Make schema validation part of acceptance criteria for integrations and AI outputs.
Use Claude to explain unfamiliar payloads in seconds.

p: When an integration breaks after a release, the cause is often a JSON shape change: a field renamed, a number sent as a string, null where an object was expected. Ask for real sample payloads in bug reports and compare them against the agreed schema. Claude can diff two JSON payloads and point out differences in seconds.

JSON also matters for AI: when a model must return data that software uses, ask engineering to enforce a schema with structured outputs and to validate before saving. Treat 'the model returned bad JSON' as a design gap, not bad luck.

mis: JSON is only for JavaScript.
It's language-neutral and used everywhere.
Order of keys matters.
Object key order generally doesn't carry meaning.
Empty string and null are the same.
They mean different things and are often handled differently.

quiz: Object vs array?
Object holds named fields in {}; array holds an ordered list in [].
What's wrong with {'a': 1}?
JSON requires double quotes.
Why validate AI outputs against a schema?
Models can return malformed or incomplete JSON; validation catches it before it breaks systems.
How would you represent 'no owner yet'?
"owner": null.
What is nesting?
Placing objects or arrays inside other objects.

sections.h: More than one way to talk
p: REST is the default, but not the only API style. Each style fits a different need, and choosing well saves months of rework.

table: Public and partner APIs, most CRUD
Can need many calls for one screen
One endpoint; client asks for exactly the fields it wants
Complex UIs, mobile on slow networks
Caching, security and cost controls are harder
Binary messages from a strict contract (protocol buffers)

p: Public partner API: REST, because everyone understands it and tooling is universal.
Live chat: WebSockets, because polling every second wastes resources and still feels laggy.
Internal calls between 40 microservices: gRPC, for speed and strict contracts.
A mobile app whose screens combine data from many sources: GraphQL, so one request returns exactly what the screen needs.

When an AI chat shows words appearing gradually, it uses streaming, often Server-Sent Events over HTTP. This matters for perceived speed: users see the first words in under a second even if the full answer takes ten.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Capture the API style decision and reasons in an architecture decision record.
For GraphQL, ask how query cost and abuse will be controlled.
For real-time features, ask how many concurrent connections are expected.

p: API style debates can consume weeks. Bring structure: list consumers (public partners, internal services, mobile, browser), traffic patterns (request/response vs live updates) and team skills. Record the decision and trade-offs in an architecture decision record so the debate doesn't restart every quarter.

For real-time features such as live order tracking or collaborative editing, ask early about scale: how many simultaneous connections, how frequent updates are, and what happens on reconnect. These drive infrastructure cost and are easy to underestimate.

mis: GraphQL replaces REST.
They coexist; each fits different needs.
WebSockets are needed for any 'live' feature.
Polling every 30 seconds may be fine for slowly changing data.
gRPC is only for big tech.
It's common in any microservice architecture needing fast internal calls.

gloss: Query language letting clients pick fields.
Compact binary data format used by gRPC.
Sending a response in pieces as it's produced.

quiz: Why not REST polling for chat?
It wastes requests and adds delay; WebSockets push messages instantly.
Main GraphQL benefit for mobile?
Fetch exactly the needed fields in one request.
Where is gRPC typically used?
Internal service-to-service communication.
What does streaming improve in AI chat?
Perceived speed, since text appears immediately.
One GraphQL risk?
Expensive or abusive queries without cost limits.

sections.h: Don't call us, we'll call you
p: With a normal API, your system asks another system for updates. With a webhook, the other system tells you the moment something happens by sending an HTTP request to a URL you gave it. Payment providers, CRMs, GitHub and form tools all use webhooks. It's the difference between checking your mailbox every ten minutes and getting a doorbell.

flow: provider POSTs JSON to your URL
steps: You give the provider a URL and choose events.
Something happens; the provider sends a POST with a JSON payload.
Your system checks the signature to confirm it's genuine.
You reply 200 quickly; heavy work goes to a queue.
If you don't reply, the provider retries, so you may receive the same event more than once.

p: Because webhooks retry, the same 'payment succeeded' message can arrive twice. If your system ships the order twice or credits the account twice, that's a real loss. An idempotent handler produces the same result whether a message is processed once or five times, usually by storing each event ID and skipping ones already seen.
In HTTP terms, GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by design; POST is not. Payment APIs add idempotency keys so a retried POST doesn't charge twice.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: For any payment or financial integration, ask 'what happens if this event arrives twice?'.
Ask for a nightly reconciliation that compares provider records with yours.
Include webhook monitoring and alerting in the definition of done.

p: Webhook problems surface as data mismatches: an order marked unpaid while the payment provider shows paid, or a CRM record missing. Ask for a reconciliation process from day one: a scheduled job that compares records and flags differences. It turns silent data drift into a visible, fixable queue.

When integrating automation tools like Zapier or n8n, you'll configure webhooks yourself. Test what happens when the same event is sent twice, when your endpoint is down, and when payloads arrive out of order. Those three tests catch most production issues.

mis: Webhooks are delivered exactly once.
Most providers deliver at least once, so duplicates happen.
Webhooks arrive in order.
Order isn't guaranteed; handle out-of-order events.
Anyone can't call my webhook URL.
Without signature checks, anyone who finds it can.

gloss: An HTTP callback sent when an event occurs.
Safe to repeat with the same result.
A unique ID that prevents duplicate processing.
Comparing two systems' records to find mismatches.

quiz: Webhook vs polling?
Webhooks push events when they happen; polling repeatedly asks.
Why do duplicates happen?
Providers retry when they don't get a timely acknowledgement.
How do you make a handler idempotent?
Record each event ID and skip ones already processed.
Is POST idempotent?
No, which is why payment APIs use idempotency keys.
Why reply 200 before heavy work?
To avoid timeouts that trigger retries.

p: Authentication (AuthN) answers 'who are you?'. Authorization (AuthZ) answers 'what are you allowed to do?'. At an office: your badge proves who you are; the access list decides which floors it opens. Many serious breaches are authorization failures: a logged-in user seeing someone else's data by changing an ID in the URL.

steps: User proves identity with a password, a one-time code, a passkey or SSO.
The server stores 'this session belongs to Asha' and gives the browser a cookie with the session ID.
Alternatively the server issues a signed token containing claims such as user ID, role and expiry. Any server can verify the signature without a database lookup.
The cookie or token is sent along; the server checks it, then checks permissions.
Short-lived access tokens are renewed with a longer-lived refresh token, limiting damage if one leaks.

p: A JWT looks like xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz: a header (algorithm), a payload (claims like sub: user-42, role: manager, exp: expiry time) and a signature. The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it: never put secrets in a JWT. The signature makes it tamper-proof.

table: Can see records for own region only

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Write permission rules into requirements as a role/permission matrix.
Ask for tests that try to access another user's record (IDOR testing).
For AI agents, decide whose permissions the agent acts with; this is a top security question.

p: Security reviews and enterprise questionnaires ask how access is controlled. A role/permission matrix (rows: roles; columns: actions; cells: allowed/denied) is the clearest artefact you can own. It also becomes the basis for test cases, including negative tests that try forbidden actions.

Authorization bugs often hide in plain sight: changing /invoices/1001 to /invoices/1002 in the URL and seeing someone else's invoice. Ask QA and security to test this explicitly (it's called IDOR, insecure direct object reference), especially for multi-tenant products where one customer must never see another's data.

mis: If login is secure, the app is secure.
Most data leaks come from authorization flaws after login.
JWTs are encrypted.
They're signed, not encrypted; anyone can read the payload.
Long sessions are user-friendly and harmless.
Long-lived tokens increase damage if stolen.

gloss: Server-side record of a logged-in user.

quiz: Badge vs floor access maps to?
Badge is authentication; floor access is authorization.
Can anyone read a JWT payload?
Yes, it's encoded not encrypted; only the signature protects integrity.
Why use short-lived access tokens?
To limit the damage if one is stolen.
What is RBAC?
Permissions assigned to roles, and users given roles.
Biggest new AuthZ question with AI agents?
Whose permissions the agent uses and how actions are limited.

sections.h: Letting apps act for you, safely
p: When an app asks 'Allow Calendly to view your Google Calendar?', that's OAuth 2.0. It lets one app get limited access to your data in another app without ever seeing your password. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds a standard way to log in on top of OAuth. SSO (single sign-on) lets employees use one company login for all work apps, managed by an identity provider like Okta, Microsoft Entra ID or Google Workspace.

steps: Resource owner (you), client (the app), authorization server (Google login), resource server (Calendar API).
The specific permissions requested, like read-only calendar. Good apps ask for the minimum.
An access token (short-lived) to call APIs and a refresh token to get new ones.
You can withdraw access any time without changing your password.

p: Enterprise customers want employees to log in with company credentials so IT can enforce MFA and remove access when someone leaves. Two protocols dominate: SAML (older, XML-based, very common in enterprises) and OIDC (modern, JSON-based). Supporting both is often a sales requirement. Related: SCIM automatically creates and removes user accounts from the company directory.

sections.h: Where it shows up for you now
table: 'Sign in with Google' on your product
An MCP connector in Claude accesses your Drive

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Scope SSO as its own epic: SAML, OIDC, SCIM, admin settings, testing with real customer IdPs.
Review OAuth scopes for least privilege, especially for AI integrations.
Plan what happens when a token is revoked mid-workflow.

p: SSO requests are common in enterprise sales and often under-scoped. A realistic SSO epic includes SAML and OIDC support, per-customer configuration screens, just-in-time user creation or SCIM provisioning, handling of users who leave, testing with each customer's identity provider, and support runbooks. Plan customer onboarding time too; IT teams move slowly.

OAuth is central to AI tooling. When you connect Claude to Google Drive or a CRM through a connector, you're granting OAuth scopes. Review scopes with the same care as giving a new contractor system access: least privilege, revocable, and logged.

mis: OAuth is a login protocol.
OAuth is for delegated access; login is OIDC on top.
SSO means less security.
SSO usually improves security through central MFA and offboarding.
Once connected, integrations need no review.
Tokens and scopes should be reviewed and revoked when no longer needed.

gloss: Service that authenticates users, e.g. Okta.
