quiz: Does the client app ever see your Google password in OAuth?
No, you log in at Google; the app only gets a token.
OAuth vs OIDC?
OAuth grants access to resources; OIDC adds a standard way to authenticate users.
Why do enterprises insist on SSO?
Central control: MFA, policies and instant removal of leavers.
What are scopes?
The specific permissions an app requests.
What does SCIM do?
Automatically provisions and de-provisions user accounts.

p: Almost every product's most valuable asset is its data, and how it's stored shapes what's easy and what's painful. Relational (SQL) databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL store data in tables with strict columns, like well-governed spreadsheets linked together. NoSQL is a family of alternatives: document stores like MongoDB keep flexible JSON-like documents; key-value stores like Redis keep simple lookups in memory for speed.
SQL: a projects table and a tasks table, each task with a project_id linking back. Reporting 'all overdue tasks by project' is one query. Changing the structure needs a migration.

MongoDB: one project document containing an array of task objects. Reading a project with all its tasks is one fast lookup, and adding a new field needs no migration. But a report across all projects is harder, and duplicated data can drift out of sync.
Most companies use both: PostgreSQL as the source of truth, Redis for caching, sometimes a document or vector store for specific features.
Modern PostgreSQL also stores JSON and vectors, which is why many teams default to it.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask what the source of truth is for each important entity.
Be wary of NoSQL for transactional data without a strong reason.
Remember finance and analytics teams need to query the data too.

p: Database choices show up in architecture reviews, vendor evaluations and data platform discussions. A practical question set: what's the source of truth for each entity, how will finance and analytics query it, what consistency is needed (can we tolerate a few seconds of stale data?), and who operates it. Those answers usually make the choice obvious.

Watch for 'we'll use MongoDB because it's flexible' on transactional systems. Flexibility is real, but payments, inventory and ledgers need strong consistency and constraints that relational databases provide by default.

mis: NoSQL means no structure.
Data still has structure; it's just enforced in the application instead of the database.
SQL databases can't scale.
They scale very far with replicas, partitioning and good design.
Redis is a database replacement.
It's mostly a fast cache and data-structure store alongside a primary database.

quiz: Best fit for payments and why?
SQL, for strict integrity and transactions.
What is Redis mostly used for?
Caching, sessions and fast lookups.
One NoSQL advantage?
Flexible schema that's easy to evolve.
One NoSQL risk?
Duplicated data drifting out of sync; harder cross-record reporting.
Can PostgreSQL store JSON?
Yes, which is one reason it's a popular default.

sections.h: Why data models matter to you
p: A data model decides what the product can and can't do. If the model says a task has one owner, 'support multiple owners' is not a UI change; it's a structural change touching data, APIs, reports and migrations. Reading an ER diagram lets you see those constraints before you promise anything.

steps: Boxes, each usually a table: Customer, Order, Product.
Fields inside a box: name, email, created_at.
The unique ID of each row, like order_id.
A field pointing to another table's PK, like order.customer_id. It creates the relationship.
Line endings (crow's foot notation) show one or many.

p: Today: tasks has owner_id (FK to users). That's 1:N: a user owns many tasks, a task has one owner.

Requirement: tasks can have several owners. That's N:M. You need a new task_owners junction table (task_id, user_id), a migration to copy existing owners into it, API changes (owner becomes owners list), UI changes, and report updates. That's why the estimate is three sprints, not three days.
Normalisation is the principle behind this: store each fact once and link to it, to avoid inconsistent duplicates.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask for the ERD in design reviews and walk new requirements against it.
Turn 'can X have many Y?' questions into explicit cardinality decisions early.
Use Claude to generate and explain ERDs from a description or schema (as a Mermaid diagram).

p: Bring the ERD to refinement sessions. When a stakeholder asks 'can a project belong to two programmes?' or 'can a user be in multiple teams?', you can check cardinality on the spot and flag structural changes before they're promised. This is one of the highest-leverage technical habits a TPM can build.

You can also reverse-engineer ERDs: paste a database schema or a list of tables into Claude and ask for a Mermaid ER diagram plus a plain-English explanation. Then explain it back and ask Claude to correct you.

mis: ERDs are only for database designers.
They're the clearest map of what the product can and can't represent.
Many-to-many can be stored with a list in one column.
That breaks querying and integrity; use a junction table.
Primary keys should be meaningful (like email).
Stable, meaningless IDs avoid problems when values change.

gloss: How many of one entity relate to another.

quiz: Customer and orders: which relationship?
One-to-many.
How is many-to-many stored?
With a junction table holding both foreign keys.
Where does the FK go in 1:N?
On the 'many' side table.
Why is 'multiple owners' a big change?
It changes cardinality, requiring a new table, migration, API and UI changes.
What is a primary key?
A unique identifier for each row.

p: Applications ask databases questions in SQL: 'give me all overdue tasks for user 42'. How fast the answer comes back depends far more on how data is indexed and queried than on how big the server is.

steps: Combine rows from related tables, like tasks joined to users to show owner names.
A sorted lookup structure on one or more columns. Like a book index, it avoids reading every page. Without one, the database does a full table scan.
Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes and use storage, so you add them for real query patterns.
EXPLAIN shows how the database will run a query: index used or full scan.
Group several changes so they all succeed or all fail.

table: Debit and credit both happen, or neither
Balance never goes below the allowed limit
Two transfers at once don't corrupt balances
After 'success', a crash doesn't lose it

p: The dashboard runs 'tasks where owner = 42 and due_date < today' on 10 million rows. No index on owner_id and due_date, so the database scans all 10 million rows on every load.
Adding a composite index on (owner_id, due_date) makes it a few milliseconds. A bigger server would have cost money every month and still been slow.
Other common culprits: the N+1 problem (one query for a list, then one more per row), fetching every column when you need two, and no pagination.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: When something is slow, ask 'have we looked at the query plan?' before approving more hardware.
Ask for slow-query monitoring in production.
Treat payment and inventory flows as needing transactions; ask how failures roll back.

p: Performance escalations often arrive as requests for bigger infrastructure. Before approving spend, ask for the slow-query log and query plans. In many teams, a handful of missing indexes or N+1 patterns explain most database load. A TPM who asks the right question can save a significant chunk of cloud spend.

Transactions matter for anything involving money or inventory. In design reviews ask: what happens if step three of five fails? If the answer isn't 'everything rolls back' or 'we have a compensating action', there's a data integrity risk.

mis: More indexes always help.
Too many slow writes and waste storage.
The database is slow because it has too much data.
Usually it's how the data is queried, not how much there is.
ACID is only for banks.
Any system with orders, bookings or counts needs it.

gloss: Group of changes applied all or nothing.
Many small queries instead of one.

quiz: Why not just buy a bigger server?
Missing indexes or bad queries stay slow and costly; fixing the query is usually cheaper and faster.
Downside of indexes?
Slower writes and extra storage.
Explain atomicity.
All parts of a transaction happen, or none do.
What does EXPLAIN show?
How the database will execute a query, including index use.
What is N+1?
One query for a list plus one per item, causing many round trips.

sections.h: Why 'just a database change' is never just that
p: Applications are tightly coupled to the shape of their data. Rename a column and every piece of code, report and integration that reads it breaks, possibly across several services that deploy at different times. That's why database changes need careful sequencing and rollback plans.

steps: A library that maps database rows to code objects (Prisma, Hibernate, Django ORM; ODMs for document databases). Developers write code instead of raw SQL.
Versioned scripts that change the schema step by step, each with a way back.
Reusing a fixed set of database connections; without it, traffic spikes exhaust the database.
Regular snapshots plus logs allowing point-in-time recovery to a specific minute.
Practising restores; an untested backup is a hope, not a plan.

sections.h: Worked example: renaming a column safely
p: Goal: rename customer_name to full_name, used by 3 services. Zero downtime means 'expand and contract':

1) Add the new column full_name. 2) Write to both columns. 3) Backfill old rows. 4) Switch services to read full_name, one by one. 5) Stop writing the old column. 6) Drop customer_name a release later.
Six steps across several releases, each safe to roll back. Doing it in one step would break whichever service deploys last.

table: Long migration locks a big table
Run in batches, off-peak, with online tools
Tested rollback script, backup taken just before

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Every release with a migration needs a named rollback plan and a backup checkpoint.
Ask 'is this migration backward compatible with the currently running code?'.
Schedule restore drills; ask for the last successful one.

p: Release readiness reviews should explicitly ask about database migrations: Is it backward compatible? How long will it run on production-sized data? Can it run online? What's the rollback? When was the backup taken? Many post-mortems trace back to a migration that worked on small test data and locked a large production table.

Restore drills are a cheap insurance policy. Ask quarterly: when did we last restore production data into a test environment, how long did it take, and did anything fail? The answer often reveals that recovery time objectives in contracts are not actually achievable.

mis: The ORM handles everything, so SQL knowledge is unnecessary.
ORMs can generate inefficient queries; someone must understand the SQL.
Backups exist, so we're safe.
Untested backups may fail when needed.
Migrations can always be reversed.
Destructive changes like dropping columns lose data permanently.

gloss: Maps database rows to code objects.

quiz: Why is renaming a column risky?
Every consumer reading the old name breaks, and services deploy at different times.
What is expand and contract?
Add new structure, migrate gradually, then remove the old.
Why test restores?
Backups can be corrupt or incomplete; only a restore proves them.
What problem does connection pooling solve?
Running out of database connections under load.
What must every migration release have?
A tested rollback plan and a recent backup.

p: Growth eventually strains a single database: too many reads, too much data, too many writes. There are three main responses, in rising order of cost and complexity.

table: Copies of the primary that serve reads
Splitting a big table into parts within one database (e.g. by month)
Spreading data across many databases by a key (e.g. customer region)

p: Replicas copy changes from the primary, usually within milliseconds but sometimes seconds. A user who saves a setting and immediately reloads might read from a replica that hasn't caught up and see the old value. Teams handle this by reading your own writes from the primary.

Cheapest first: find slow queries and add indexes. Then add caching (Redis) for repeated reads. Then add read replicas for reporting and read-heavy pages. Then partition the biggest tables. Only then consider sharding, which changes how every query is routed and often takes quarters.
Choosing a shard key badly, for example by customer when one customer is 40% of traffic, creates a 'hot shard' and the problem returns.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Push for the cheapest fixes first, with data.
If sharding is needed, plan it as a programme with feature-freeze trade-offs agreed with product.
Track replication lag as an operational metric.

p: Scaling projects compete with feature work for months, so they need business framing: what growth triggers them, what risk they remove (outages, slow pages), and what it costs to wait. Present options as a ladder from cheap to expensive, with metrics showing when each rung is needed.

Replication lag creates puzzling bugs: 'I saved but it didn't save'. When support reports intermittent stale data right after updates, ask whether reads go to replicas. The fix is usually routing that user's next reads to the primary.

mis: Sharding is the standard first step for scale.
It's usually the last, most expensive step.
Read replicas help with write load.
They only offload reads.
Replication is a backup.
Replicas copy mistakes too; you still need backups.

gloss: The database instance that accepts writes.
Delay before replicas show new writes.
One slice of data on its own database.
The field used to decide where data goes.

quiz: Order of options from cheapest?
Query/index fixes, caching, read replicas, partitioning, sharding.
What's replication lag in user terms?
Seeing old data right after saving.
What is a hot shard?
One shard receiving disproportionate traffic.
Partitioning vs sharding?
Partitioning splits within one database; sharding across many.
Why is sharding expensive?
It changes data routing for the entire application.

p: Computers find each other by IP address, but people use names. DNS (Domain Name System) translates names like shop.example.com into addresses. It's distributed and heavily cached, which makes it fast and resilient, and also explains why changes take time to appear everywhere.

flow: IP address, cached for the TTL
steps: Where you buy the domain (GoDaddy, Cloudflare, etc.). It records which nameservers are in charge.
Servers holding your DNS records, often at Cloudflare, AWS Route 53 or the registrar.
A (name → IPv4), AAAA (→ IPv6), CNAME (alias to another name), MX (mail servers), TXT (verification, email security), SOA (zone admin details).
Time to live: how many seconds resolvers may cache an answer.

sections.h: Worked example: moving to a new host on Saturday
p: If the A record's TTL is 86,400 seconds (24 hours), some users will hit the old server for up to a day after you change it.

So: on Thursday lower the TTL to 300 seconds. Wait for the old TTL to expire. On Saturday change the record; within about five minutes nearly everyone moves. Keep the old server running until traffic drains. After it's stable, raise the TTL again.
That's why 'DNS propagation' is plannable rather than mysterious.

table: CNAME pointing to a deleted cloud resource

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Put TTL lowering in cut-over plans 24–48 hours ahead.
Own a register of domains, renewal dates and auto-renew status.
Make sure DNS access is restricted and changes are logged.

p: DNS appears in launches, rebrands, migrations and incident post-mortems. Keep a domain register: every domain, registrar, renewal date, auto-renew status, DNS provider and owner. Expired domains and forgotten records have taken down well-known products.

For cut-overs, put DNS steps in the runbook with times: TTL lowered (T–48h), record changed (T), verification from several locations (T+5m), rollback criteria, and TTL restored (T+7d). This turns DNS from a source of anxiety into a routine step.

mis: DNS changes are instant.
They depend on TTL and caching.
Propagation takes 48 hours no matter what.
With low TTLs prepared in advance, minutes.
The registrar and DNS provider must be the same.
They're often different services.

gloss: System mapping names to IP addresses.
Cache duration for a DNS answer.
Time for changes to be seen everywhere.

quiz: Why lower TTL before a migration?
So cached old answers expire quickly after the change.
What does an MX record do?
Says which servers receive email for the domain.
CNAME vs A record?
A points to an IP; CNAME points to another name.
Who holds your DNS records?
The authoritative nameservers.
One preventable DNS outage?
An expired domain because renewal was missed.

p: Email was designed without proof of sender, so spammers can pretend to be anyone. Big inbox providers (Gmail, Outlook) now check three DNS-based records to decide whether your mail is genuine. If they're missing or wrong, your password resets and invoices land in spam or vanish, and Gmail and Yahoo now require them for bulk senders.

table: Is this server allowed to send for this domain?
Was this message really signed by the domain and unchanged?
Cryptographic signature checked with a public key in DNS
What should receivers do if SPF/DKIM fail, and who gets reports?

p: Marketing moves newsletters to a new provider, and the product team moves transactional email to another. If SPF still only lists the old provider, and DKIM isn't set up for the new ones, messages fail checks. With DMARC set to reject, they're blocked entirely.
Fix: add each provider to SPF, publish their DKIM keys, start DMARC at p=none to monitor reports, then tighten to quarantine and reject once everything passes.
In Gmail, open a message and choose Show original. You'll see SPF: PASS, DKIM: PASS, DMARC: PASS, or a failure. That's the fastest triage step for 'customers aren't receiving our emails'.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Add email authentication to launch checklists for any new sending tool.
Coordinate marketing, IT and engineering, who often each own one piece.
Monitor DMARC reports for unknown senders.

p: Email deliverability problems are often discovered by customer complaints weeks after a tooling change. Add a checklist item for any new email-sending service: SPF updated, DKIM published, DMARC reports reviewed, test emails checked in Gmail and Outlook headers.

Ownership is usually split: IT owns the domain, marketing owns newsletter tools, engineering owns transactional email. A TPM can make one person accountable for email authentication and set up DMARC reporting to a shared inbox or tool.

mis: Spam folder means bad content.
Often it's failed authentication, not content.
SPF alone is enough.
DKIM and DMARC are needed for reliable delivery today.
DMARC reject should be set immediately.
Start with monitoring to avoid blocking legitimate mail.

gloss: List of servers allowed to send.
Signature proving the message is authentic.

quiz: What does SPF list?
Servers and services allowed to send email for the domain.
What does DKIM prove?
The message was signed by the domain and not altered.
Safest DMARC starting policy?
p=none, to monitor before enforcing.
Fastest triage step?
Check SPF/DKIM/DMARC results in the message headers.
Why do provider switches break email?
New senders aren't authorised in SPF or signed with DKIM.

p: Every device on a network has an IP address so data can find it. IPv4 addresses look like 203.0.113.25; there are about 4.3 billion, which ran out. IPv6 addresses look like 2001:db8::1 and are practically unlimited. Most networks run both.

A bank will only accept API calls from IP addresses on its allow-list. Your app runs on autoscaling cloud servers whose IPs change. Solution: route outbound traffic through a NAT gateway with a fixed (static/elastic) IP and give the bank that address.
Also note: the bank's firewall must allow your webhook calls to reach you, and vice versa. Changes on either side usually need change requests with lead time.
Your home router lets many private devices share one public IP, translating addresses as traffic goes out. Cloud NAT gateways do the same for private servers.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Capture IP allow-listing needs early in enterprise integrations; they cause late surprises.
Keep a register of static IPs shared with partners.
Plan change windows when IPs change.

p: IP allow-listing is a classic late blocker in enterprise and banking integrations. In discovery, ask: does the client restrict inbound or outbound traffic by IP? Do we need static IPs? What's their change process and lead time? Getting this in week one avoids a go-live delay in week twelve.
Cloud architecture changes can silently change IPs. Keep a register of IPs shared with partners, and make 'does this change our outbound IPs?' a question in change reviews.

mis: Every server has one fixed IP.
Cloud servers often get new IPs when replaced or scaled.
Private IPs are secure by themselves.
They reduce exposure but still need access controls.
IPv6 is rare now.
It's widely used, especially on mobile networks.

gloss: Translating private addresses to a public one.

quiz: Why does IPv6 exist?
IPv4 addresses ran out.
Why do banks want static IPs?
To allow-list exactly who can call them.
Is 192.168.1.5 public?
No, it's a private range.
How can autoscaled servers present one fixed IP?
Route outbound traffic through a NAT gateway with a static IP.
Why do allow-lists cause delays?
Firewall changes need change requests on both sides.

p: Networks work in layers. IP gets packets to the right machine. TCP or UDP decides how the data is delivered. HTTP, SSH and others are the 'languages' applications speak on top. Ports decide which program on the machine receives the data.

table: Best effort, may drop or reorder
Video calls, gaming, DNS, live streams
p: A video call prefers dropping a frame to freezing while it waits for a lost packet, so it uses UDP.
A socket is one specific connection: an IP address plus a port at each end. SSH uses key pairs rather than passwords to log in to servers securely.

A client's network team says only port 443 outbound is allowed. That means your product must work entirely over HTTPS: no direct database connections, no custom ports, and real-time features must use WebSockets over 443. Anything else needs a firewall exception, often weeks of approval.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Collect client network constraints during discovery, not at go-live.
Ask engineering which ports the product needs and document them.
Make sure SSH access to production is limited and audited.

p: Enterprise clients often have strict network rules. Collect them during discovery: allowed ports, proxies, SSL inspection, IP restrictions. Then confirm with engineering that the product works under those constraints, ideally with a test from inside a similar network.

For production access, ask how engineers connect to servers: SSH with personal keys, through a bastion host, via SSO-backed access tools? Auditors will ask, and shared credentials are a common finding.

mis: TCP is always better because it's reliable.
For real-time media, late data is useless; UDP fits better.
Ports are physical sockets.
Network ports are numbers in software.
SSH passwords are fine.
Key-based or SSO-based access is the norm.

gloss: Number identifying a service on a machine.

quiz: Why do video calls use UDP?
Speed matters more than perfect delivery; late packets are useless.
Which port is HTTPS?
What's SSH for?
Securely logging in to and managing servers.
Implication of 'only 443 outbound'?
Everything must run over HTTPS; other ports need exceptions.
What is a socket?
A specific connection defined by IP and port on both ends.

p: HTTPS means the connection between browser and server is encrypted with TLS, so nobody in between, like public Wi-Fi or an ISP, can read or alter it. TLS replaced the older SSL, though people still say 'SSL certificate'. Browsers mark plain HTTP sites as 'Not secure'.

steps: The server presents a certificate proving it owns the domain, signed by a trusted certificate authority (CA) such as Let's Encrypt or DigiCert.
Browser and server agree encryption keys using public-key cryptography.
All data travels encrypted with those keys.
Certificates expire (often 90 days to 1 year) and must be renewed, ideally automatically.

sections.h: Worked example: the expired certificate outage
p: At midnight a certificate on api.example.com expires. Browsers show full-page security warnings, mobile apps refuse to connect, and partner integrations fail. Nothing in the code changed, yet everything is down.
Prevention: automatic renewal (ACME/Let's Encrypt or cloud-managed certificates), an inventory of every certificate and its expiry, and alerts 30, 14 and 7 days out.

table: TLS 1.2+ everywhere, HTTP redirected to HTTPS

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Maintain a certificate inventory with owners and expiry dates.
Make expiry alerts part of operational readiness.
Know your TLS answers for client security questionnaires.

p: Expired certificates are one of the most avoidable outage types. A simple control: a shared inventory with domain, certificate type, issuer, expiry, renewal method and owner, plus automated monitoring with alerts. Cloud-managed certificates renew automatically; ones manually installed on servers or third-party devices are the risk.
Security questionnaires ask about encryption in transit and at rest. Keep a standard answer set agreed with your security team so sales and delivery don't improvise.

mis: HTTPS means the site is trustworthy.
It means the connection is encrypted; scam sites can have certificates too.
Certificates last for years.
Many now last 90 days; the industry is moving to even shorter lifetimes.
Internal traffic doesn't need encryption.
Zero Trust and compliance often require encryption inside networks too.

gloss: Proof a server owns a domain.

quiz: SSL vs TLS?
TLS is the modern successor; 'SSL' is the old name still used informally.
What happens if a certificate expires?
Browsers and apps refuse secure connections, causing outages.
How to prevent expiry outages?
Automatic renewal plus inventory and alerts.
What does a CA do?
Verifies domain ownership and signs certificates.
What does HTTPS protect against?
Eavesdropping and tampering in transit.

p: Browsers block a web page from reading responses from a different origin (domain, protocol or port) unless that server explicitly allows it. This same-origin policy stops a malicious site from quietly reading your bank data using your logged-in session. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server says 'this other origin is allowed'.

steps: For many requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission.
The API replies with headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com.
If allowed, the real request proceeds; if not, the browser blocks it and shows a CORS error.
p: Key point: CORS is enforced by the browser but configured on the server. The frontend team cannot fix it alone.

table: Routing, SSL termination, caching, rate limiting, hiding servers
p: Nginx, HAProxy, Cloudflare and cloud load balancers all act as reverse proxies. A reverse proxy can also solve CORS by serving frontend and API from the same origin.

sections.h: Worked example: CORS errors two days before launch
p: The new frontend on app.example.com can't call the API. Fix options: backend adds the frontend's origin to its CORS allow-list (fastest), or a reverse proxy serves the API under app.example.com/api so there's no cross-origin call. Don't allow '*' with credentials; that's a security hole.

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Route CORS errors to the backend/API owner, not the frontend.
Add allowed origins per environment (dev, staging, prod) to the release checklist.
Ask what the reverse proxy does in your architecture: it often holds critical config.

p: CORS errors typically appear when a new frontend, domain or environment is introduced. Add 'allowed origins configured for each environment' to the environment setup checklist. When a CORS ticket lands, route it to the API owner with the exact origin and error text.

Reverse proxies often hold important configuration: routing rules, timeouts, upload size limits, rate limits. When an issue only appears in production ('large uploads fail', 'requests time out at 60 seconds'), ask what the proxy is configured to do.

mis: CORS is a server security feature.
It's a browser rule; server-to-server calls ignore it.
The frontend can disable CORS.
Only the server can allow cross-origin access.
Allowing all origins is harmless.
With credentials it exposes users to attacks.

gloss: Mechanism to allow specific cross-origin access.
Server in front of your servers.

quiz: Who must fix a CORS error?
The server/API owner, by configuring allowed origins.
Why does the same-origin policy exist?
To stop malicious sites reading data using your session.
Forward vs reverse proxy?
Forward sits in front of users; reverse in front of servers.
How can a proxy remove CORS issues?
By serving frontend and API from the same origin.
Why avoid '*' with credentials?
It would let any site make authenticated requests.

p: Between users and your application servers sit layers that make the system fast, available and safe. Most incident timelines mention at least one of them.

sections.flowLabel: Typical request path through edge layers
steps: A global network of servers caching your images, scripts and pages close to users. A user in Chennai gets files from a nearby city rather than from Virginia. Cache hit: served from the edge; miss: fetched from your origin.
Spreads requests across several servers using algorithms like round robin or least connections, and runs health checks to stop sending traffic to unhealthy servers (failover).

A network firewall allows or blocks traffic by address and port. A WAF inspects web requests for attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Many providers add DDoS protection and bot management.

p: Traffic will triple for a sale. Checklist with the team: CDN caching rules for product images and static pages (fewer origin hits); load balancer health checks and autoscaling limits; WAF rate limits that block bots without blocking real shoppers; a plan to purge the CDN cache when prices change; and who watches dashboards during the event.

table: Site slow worldwide but fine locally
No CDN, or low cache hit rate

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Include CDN purge, WAF rules and load balancer config in release and event plans.
Ask for cache hit ratio and WAF block metrics on dashboards.
Know who can change these settings in an emergency.

p: Peak-event readiness (sales, launches, enrolment periods) is a classic TPM responsibility. Build a checklist with each team: expected traffic, CDN cache rules and purge process, WAF and rate-limit rules, autoscaling limits, database headroom, third-party limits, dashboards and a war-room roster.

After incidents, ask which layer handled what. Did the CDN absorb traffic? Did the WAF block bots or real users? Was a server failing health checks still in rotation? These answers drive the follow-up actions.

mis: A CDN is only for images.
CDNs also cache pages and APIs and provide security.
A load balancer prevents all downtime.
It only helps if there are healthy servers behind it.
A WAF makes the app secure.
It's a filter; the code must still be secure.

gloss: Your actual servers behind the CDN.
Served from cache vs fetched from origin.
Regular test that a server is working.

quiz: Why is a CDN faster?
Content is served from a server close to the user.
What do health checks do?
Detect unhealthy servers so traffic avoids them.
Firewall vs WAF?
Firewall filters by address/port; WAF inspects web requests for attacks.
Users see stale prices. Likely cause?
CDN cache not purged after the update.
Name a WAF risk during a sale.
Rules blocking real customers.

sections.h: Keeping important things off the internet
p: In the cloud, you build your own private network (AWS calls it a VPC, Azure a VNet). Inside it you create subnets. Public subnets can be reached from the internet; private subnets can't. The golden rule: put only the front door (load balancers) in public subnets, and keep application servers and especially databases private.

steps: Rules saying where traffic from a subnet goes.
Connects public subnets to the internet.
Lets private servers make outbound calls (updates, third-party APIs) without being reachable inbound.
Firewall rules per resource, e.g. database accepts port 5432 only from app servers.
Encrypted tunnel letting staff or partner networks reach private resources.

sections.h: Worked example: a private connection request
p: A large client wants to reach your platform without using the public internet. Options to explore with engineering: site-to-site VPN, cloud private connectivity (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link), or dedicated links. Each has different cost, lead time and support burden, so it's a commercial as well as technical decision.
Many companies are replacing VPNs for staff access with Zero Trust access, which checks identity and device for each application instead of opening the whole network.

table: No, private subnet, access only from app tier
Through SSO-backed bastion/Zero Trust with audit logs

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Ask for a network diagram showing public vs private placement.
Treat private connectivity requests as scoped deals with cost and lead time.
NAT gateways and data transfer are common hidden cloud costs; ask about them.

p: Network diagrams are a staple of security reviews. Ask for one showing internet gateway, public and private subnets, where each component lives, and allowed traffic between them. If a database sits in a public subnet or has a public IP, raise it immediately.

Cloud bills often surprise teams with networking costs: NAT gateway hourly and per-GB charges, cross-zone and cross-region data transfer. When reviewing cloud spend, ask for a breakdown of data transfer; it's frequently a top-five line item.

mis: Private subnet means no internet at all.
Private servers can reach out through NAT; they just can't be reached.
A VPN means full security.
It opens network access; per-app controls are still needed.
Networking is free in the cloud.
Data transfer and NAT can be significant costs.

gloss: Your private network in the cloud.
Outbound-only internet access for private servers.
Encrypted tunnel into a private network.
Verify every access request, never trust the network alone.

quiz: Where should the database live?
In a private subnet, reachable only from the app tier.
What does a NAT gateway allow?
Outbound internet access without inbound exposure.
What's a security group?
Firewall rules attached to a cloud resource.
VPN vs Zero Trust?
VPN opens network access; Zero Trust checks each app access by identity and device.
One hidden cloud networking cost?
NAT gateway and data transfer charges.

p: A large language model is a neural network trained on an enormous amount of text with one goal: predict the next token (roughly, the next word-piece). That's it. Trained at huge scale, that simple objective produces something that can summarise, translate, write code, reason through problems and follow instructions.

Physically, a model is a very large file of numbers called parameters or weights (billions of them), plus code that runs it. The weights encode patterns from the training data. The model doesn't look facts up; it generates what is most plausible given what it has seen. That explains both its power and its main weakness: fluent, confident answers that can be wrong.

table: Your own work: drafting, analysis, learning
Your software sends text, gets text back
AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure
p: An API call is just an HTTPS request: you send your API key, the model name, your instructions and the conversation, and receive the model's reply as JSON.

sections.h: Worked example: your first API call
steps: In Google AI Studio choose Get API key. Treat it like a password: never paste it into documents, chats or code you share.
Type a prompt, adjust settings like temperature, see the answer.
Click Get code to see the same request as a few lines of Python or a curl command.
Paste the code (without the key) and ask Claude to explain each line: endpoint, headers, model name, contents, response.
p: You've now seen that 'an AI feature' is an ordinary API integration with unusual behaviour: non-deterministic, token-priced, and able to be wrong.

table: Exact facts it hasn't been given
Knowing anything after its training cut-off
Being consistent run to run without controls

sections.h: What a TPM should do with this
bullets: Frame AI features as integrations with probabilistic output: plan for evaluation, fallbacks and human review.
Protect API keys: store them in a secrets manager, rotate them, never commit them to code.
Choose access path (direct API, cloud platform, open model) based on data, cost and compliance.

p: In your first AI project meetings, people will use 'the model', 'the API', 'the platform' and 'the app' interchangeably. Clarify early: which model and version, accessed how (direct API, cloud platform, self-hosted), and wrapped by what (your backend, a vendor product). Each layer has different owners, contracts and failure modes.

Treat AI features like any external integration plus a quality risk. Your plan needs: API access and keys managed as secrets, rate limits and costs understood, an evaluation set to measure quality, fallback behaviour when the model is wrong or unavailable, and monitoring. That checklist alone puts you ahead of most first AI projects.

mis: The model looks things up on the internet.
Only if the app gives it a search tool; otherwise it answers from training and the provided context.
The same prompt always gives the same answer.
Outputs vary unless settings and design constrain them.
Bigger models are always better.
Smaller models are often faster, cheaper and good enough for simple steps.

gloss: The learned numbers inside a model.
Running a model to get an output.
Secret credential for calling an API.

quiz: What is an LLM trained to do?
Predict the next token in text.
Why can LLMs be confidently wrong?
They generate plausible text rather than looking up facts.
Chat app vs API?
Chat is for people; the API lets software use the model inside products.
How should API keys be handled?
As secrets: never shared, stored in a secrets manager, rotated.
Name two limits of LLMs.
Facts after their cut-off and exact facts not in context; also arithmetic without tools.

sections.h: Three stages of making a model
p: Building a modern assistant model happens in stages. Understanding them explains knowledge cut-offs, why models sound helpful, and why 'train our own ChatGPT' is rarely sensible.

steps: The model reads trillions of tokens (web pages, books, code) and learns to predict the next token. This takes months on thousands of GPUs and costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars. The result is a base model: knowledgeable but not yet a helpful assistant; it just continues text.
Trainers write example conversations showing ideal answers. The model learns to respond like an assistant.
People compare pairs of answers and pick the better one. The model is tuned to produce preferred answers: more helpful, honest and safe. Variants use AI feedback or written principles.
Safety testing, benchmarks, red-teaming, then deployment.

p: Researchers found that model quality improves predictably with more parameters, more data and more compute. That's why frontier labs build ever larger training runs, and why only a handful of organisations can build frontier models. Most companies' leverage is in how they use models: prompting, retrieval, tools and evaluation.

sections.h: Worked example: 'let's train our own ChatGPT'

sections.h: The architecture behind every modern LLM
p: Before 2017, language models read text one word at a time, which was slow and forgot earlier context. The transformer, introduced in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need', processes all words in parallel and lets every word look at every other word. That made training on internet-scale data feasible, and it's the 'T' in GPT.

steps: Each token becomes an embedding: a list of numbers representing its meaning, plus information about its position.

Each token asks 'which other tokens matter for understanding me?' and blends in information from them. In 'The bank raised rates', attention links 'bank' to 'rates', so it means a financial bank, not a river bank.
Several attention 'heads' run in parallel, each picking up different relationships: grammar, references, topic.
Dozens of these attention + processing layers are stacked; each refines the representation.
The final layer scores every possible next token; one is chosen, appended, and the process repeats.

p: Picture a meeting where, before each person speaks, they glance at everyone else and pay most attention to the people whose points are relevant to theirs. Then they update their own view. Repeat that across 50 rounds and the room converges on a rich shared understanding. Attention is that 'glance and weigh' step, done in parallel for every word.

If 200 people do this daily, that's 1.34 million input tokens and 134,000 output tokens a day. Multiply by the model's per-million prices to get a daily cost.

p: The context window is everything the model can 'see' in one go: the system instructions, the conversation so far, any documents or tool results, and the answer it is writing. Measured in tokens, windows range from tens of thousands to around a million tokens in current frontier models. Anything not in the window does not exist for the model.

Models have no memory between separate requests. A chat 'remembers' only because the app resends the history each time. When history grows too long, apps drop or summarise older parts, which is why a long chat can 'forget' early details.

A 120-page contract is about 60,000 tokens. It fits in a large window, so you can send the whole thing and ask questions. But each question resends 60,000 tokens: slower and costlier. And models can pay less attention to details buried in the middle of very long inputs.
For one-off deep review, long context is great. For an assistant answering many questions across thousands of contracts, retrieval (RAG) is better: send only the relevant clauses.

You're helping me write a weekly status update for executives who read it in 2 minutes. Use BLUF: first line is overall status (green/amber/red) and why. Then 3 bullets: progress, risks with owner, decisions needed. Plain English, under 150 words. Notes: [paste].
p: Run it three times, score each output against your criteria, tweak, and keep the version that scores best. That's prompt engineering: brief, test, improve.

p: Start a prompt library this week: status reports, RAID log updates, meeting summaries, stakeholder emails, PRD reviews, estimation challenges. For each, keep the prompt, an example input, a good output and notes on what improved it. That library becomes your personal productivity system and, later, a set of team templates.

For prompts inside products, push for discipline: written success criteria, a test set of realistic inputs, scored comparisons before and after changes, and version history. Without these, prompt changes become opinion battles and silent regressions.

p: A hallucination is an output that sounds right but is false or unsupported: a made-up statistic, a non-existent policy clause, a fake citation. It happens because a model generates the most plausible continuation, not a verified fact. When it lacks the information, a plausible-sounding answer is still the most likely text.

steps: Explicitly permit and encourage the model to say when information isn't available. This alone reduces false answers a lot.
Provide the documents and instruct: answer only from these.
For long documents, ask the model to extract exact quotes first, then answer from the quotes.
Each claim must point to a source; claims without one are removed.
Run the same prompt several times (inconsistency signals hallucination), or have a second step check claims against sources.
For high-stakes outputs (legal, medical, financial), a person approves before use.

p: Without controls, a customer asks about refunds for damaged goods and the bot invents a 60-day window. The real policy is 30 days. That's a promise the company may have to honour.

With controls: the bot retrieves the refund policy, answers only from it, cites section 3.2, and if the question isn't covered says 'I can't find that in our policy; let me connect you to an agent'. A weekly sample of conversations is reviewed for accuracy.

p: Hallucination risk is the top concern in AI steering committees. Bring a structured answer: risk level by use case, controls in place (grounding, citations, refusal when unknown, human review), how you measure (sampled audits, automated groundedness scoring, user feedback) and the escalation path when errors are found.

Design the 'I don't know' experience deliberately. A good fallback (hand off to a human, link to the source, ask a clarifying question) keeps trust high. A bot that always answers confidently loses trust after the first visible mistake.

p: Grounding means making the model answer from specific trusted sources (your documents, a database, live search results) instead of from its general training memory. It turns a closed-book exam into an open-book one, and ideally the student also shows which page they used.

table: Your files via RAG or upload

p: NotebookLM only answers from the sources you upload and shows numbered citations you can click to see the exact passage. Upload three project documents and ask ten questions; check each citation. You'll notice it says when something isn't in the sources, and that answer quality depends on what you uploaded. That's grounding in action.

Faithfulness or groundedness is the share of claims in an answer that are supported by the provided sources. Evaluation tools can score it automatically by checking each claim against the retrieved text. It's distinct from correctness: an answer can be faithful to an outdated document and still be wrong, which is why source quality matters.

p: For enterprise assistants, grounding is also a governance question: which sources are approved, who owns each, how often are they reviewed, and how are outdated documents removed? A content governance plan is often the missing piece in AI assistant projects.
When demoing grounded assistants to stakeholders, show the citations and click through them. It builds trust faster than any accuracy statistic, and shows exactly where quality depends on content.

p: An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector), often hundreds or thousands long, so that texts with similar meaning have similar numbers. 'Cheap flights to Goa' and 'low-cost airfare to Goa' share few words but land close together. 'Python programming' and 'python snake' land far apart despite sharing a word.

steps: Run each document chunk through an embedding model; store the vectors.
Turn the user's question into a vector with the same model.
Measure closeness, usually cosine similarity. Closest vectors = most similar meaning.
The best matches feed search results, RAG, recommendations or duplicate detection.

p: Imagine a map with only two dimensions: one for 'royalty' and one for 'fruitiness'. King and queen sit together high on royalty; apple and banana sit together high on fruitiness. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions capturing many aspects of meaning at once, which can't be named so neatly, but the principle is the same: nearness means similarity.

Embeddings power more than RAG: duplicate ticket detection, similar-case recommendations, clustering customer feedback into themes. Once a team has embeddings, these quick wins become cheap, which is a useful roadmap insight.

p: Keyword (lexical) search finds documents containing the exact words you typed; BM25 is the standard ranking method. Semantic search finds documents with similar meaning using embeddings. Each fails where the other shines.

Hybrid search runs both and merges the ranked lists (commonly with reciprocal rank fusion). Query 'refund policy for SKU-4471': keyword search nails the product code; semantic search finds 'returns and exchanges' sections that never use the word refund. Together they return both. Many production RAG systems add a reranker afterwards to order the combined results.

p: There are three main ways to make a general model work for your use case. Prompting changes the instructions. RAG changes what knowledge the model sees at question time. p: A neural network is layers of simple units connected by weights. Each unit takes numbers in, multiplies them by weights, adds them up, and passes the result on through an activation function. Stack many layers and the network can represent very complex patterns: recognising faces, translating languages, predicting the next word. 'Deep learning' just means many layers.

p: Imagine a sound engineer with a desk of a billion dials, trying to make every song sound right. After each song, a meter shows how far off it was, and an assistant tells them which way to nudge each dial. After enough songs, the dials settle into a configuration that works for most music. Training is that, with maths doing the nudging.

p: Executives sometimes ask why AI can't explain its decisions. The honest, simple answer: the knowledge is spread across billions of learned numbers, not written rules. Explainability tools and design choices (citations, showing sources, simple models where explanations are legally required) help.

When teams talk about training or fine-tuning, the dials analogy helps you ask about data: where do the examples come from, how are they labelled, how is quality checked? Training data quality is the biggest driver of model quality.

p: Traditional software costs little per extra user. AI features cost money on every request, priced per token, and usage grows in ways that are easy to underestimate: longer conversations, more documents in context, agents that call the model many times per task. p: Your backend should sit in the middle: it holds the API key securely, adds context, enforces permissions, logs usage, and can switch providers. Never call model APIs directly from a browser or mobile app with your key.

A bank asks where their data goes. A good answer covers: which provider and region processes the data; whether data is stored or used for training (enterprise API terms usually say no training and limited retention); encryption in transit and at rest; logging and who can access logs; and options like running through their preferred cloud region. p: Prepare an AI data-handling summary before customers ask: which providers and models, regions, retention, training use, encryption, subprocessors, logging and human access. Security and legal teams will thank you, and sales cycles speed up.

Architect for change: route every model call through your own service layer, so you can switch models for cost or quality, add a fallback during outages, and log consistently. Providers change models and prices frequently; your product shouldn't be hard-wired to one.
